title: Knowledge Spillovers, Competition, and Individual Careers
authors: Thomas Cornelissen, Christian Dustmann, Uta Schönberg
abstract: Exposure to better peers in the workplace can influence career trajectories through two opposing channels: positively, via knowledge spillovers, and negatively, through competition for advancement. We disentangle these effects by studying untrained labor market entrants and distinguishing between coworkers in the same occupation with whom they are likely to compete versus those with whom they are unlikely to compete. We find robust evidence of persistent knowledge spillovers but also identify countervailing competition effects of comparable magnitude. Both effects are more pronounced for men than for women. (JEL D83, J16, J24, M53, M54, O33)

title: Racial Promotion Gaps
authors: Deepak Hegde, Alexander Ljungqvist, Manav Raj
abstract: We study racial disparities in promotions in a setting in which promotions are formulaic: the US patent office. Using detailed administrative data that allow us to observe who is eligible for promotion when, we document that Black patent examiners experience delays in promotions they are entitled to, slowing their climb to the top of the career ladder by a year and reducing career earnings by 2.5 percent. Institutional features rule out statistical discrimination with accurate priors. Slow promotions even under Black supervisors argue against taste-based animus. Instead, the patterns fit models of belief-based discrimination. (JEL J15, J41, J71, M12, M51, O34)

title: Social Push and the Direction of Innovation
authors: Elias Einiö, Josh Feng, Xavier Jaravel
abstract: What are the implications of unequal access to innovation careers for the direction of innovation and inequality? Leveraging novel linked datasets in the United States and Finland, we document that innovators create products more likely to be purchased by consumers like them in terms of gender, socioeconomic status, and age. Homophily exists both within narrow product categories and across industries and has been stable in recent decades. Incorporating this “social push” channel into a growth model, we estimate that unequal access to innovation careers has a large effect on cost of living inequality and long-run growth. (JEL D63, J16, L26, M13, O31, O33, O47)

title: Fighting for Growth: Labor Scarcity and Technological Progress during the British Industrial Revolution
authors: Hans-Joachim Voth, Bruno Caprettini, Alex Trew
abstract: We establish a link between labor scarcity and the adoption of laborsaving technology in industrializing England. During the Napoleonic Wars, more than 10 percent of the male population served in the armed forces. Where recruitment was heavy, more machines economizing on labor were adopted. Naval recruitment, instrumented by warships' coastal access, provides exogenous variation in labor scarcity and suggests that the link between labor shortages and adoption is causal. Where mechanical skills were abundant, the impact of labor scarcity on adoption appears to be larger. (JEL J24, N13, N43, N63, N73, O14, O31)

title: A Model of the Attention Economy: Data, Platforms, and Discovery
abstract: This paper develops a dynamic model of the attention economy featuring two interlinked markets: a product market, where consumers have limited awareness of firms, and an attention market, where platforms attract attention by investing in free services (e.g., social media, streaming, podcasts) and sell targeted ads using data on consumer preferences. The model provides a tractable framework in which platform investment, ad-driven discovery, product demand, and ad revenue are jointly determined. The effects of data and interoperability policies can reverse over time, platform quality may be inefficiently high or low, and the rise of data-rich digital advertising can coincide with a declining ad revenue-to-GDP ratio. (JEL D43, D44, D58, D83, L86, M37)

title: Taxing Top Wealth: Migration Responses and Their Aggregate Economic Implications
authors: Katrine Jakobsen, Henrik Kleven, Jonas Kolsrud, Camille Landais, Mathilde Munoz
abstract: Using administrative data from Scandinavian countries, we provide evidence on international migration responses to wealth taxes and evaluate their aggregate economic implications. We find significant migration responses among the wealthy: A 1 percentage point increase in the top wealth tax rate decreases the stock of wealthy taxpayers by about 2 percent. A large fraction of the wealthy are business owners, and their businesses are negatively affected by owner out-migration. The aggregate effects are nevertheless modest: The migration responses to a 1 percentage point increase in the top wealth tax rate reduce employment by 0.02 percent, investments by 0.07 percent, and value added by 0.10 percent. (JEL D31, E22, E24, F22, H24, L26, K34)

title: Who Marries Whom? The Role of Segregation by Race and Class
authors: Benjamin Goldman, Jamie Gracie, Sonya R. Porter
abstract: Americans rarely marry outside their race or class group, a pattern with well-documented implications for inequality and intergenerational mobility. Limited exposure may partly explain these low intergroup marriage rates. We instrument for exposure using variation in childhood neighborhoods based on whether other race and class groups had more opposite-sex children of similar age. Exposure increases interclass (high- and low-parent income) marriage but has no detectable effect on interracial (White and Black) marriage. A spatial marriage model predicts that residential segregation—one of many forms of exposure—accounts for more than one-third of marital sorting by class but less than 5 percent by race. (JEL J12, J15, J62, R23)

title: Screening and Segmenting: A Consumer Surplus Perspective
authors: Dirk Bergemann, Tibor Heumann, Michael C. Wang
abstract: We analyze consumer surplus when a monopolist can adjust both prices and product qualities across segments, engaging in secondand third-degree price discrimination simultaneously. We characterize the consumer-optimal segmentation and show that it has a striking structure: Consumers with the same value receive the same quality in every segment, though prices differ. Under mild conditions, any segmentation harms consumers if and only if demand is sufficiently more elastic than supply. Hence, potential benefits for consumers depend critically on demand and supply elasticities. These findings have implications for regulatory policy regarding price discrimination and market segmentation. (JEL D42, D83, K21, L12, L15)

title: Truth Elicitation in a Nonstrategic Environment
abstract: A principal decides which party deserves a prize. Only the parties observe the state that determines who is deserving. The principal gives each party a text describing the conditions under which that party deserves the prize and asks each to report the state. The parties are nonstrategic. Each activates a known cheating procedure whose outcome depends on the state and on the text. Implementation is achieved if, whenever the parties disagree, the liar is identified by the “one-way cheating principle”: The truthful party is the unique party who could not have produced his story had the rival's story been true. (JEL D82, D91)

title: A Farewell to Public Religion? Retheorizing and Assessing the Public Relevance of Religion
authors: Damon Mayrl, Gary J. Adler, Jr., Jonathan S. Coley, Rebecca Sager, Elise Wolff, John P. Miller

title: Structural Injustice as Emergent Disorder
abstract: Structural injustice remains a puzzling concept despite its increasing prominence. I distill recent theoretical challenges into a dilemma: either structural injustice lacks the normative credentials of injustice given that wrongdoing is inessential, or it is redundant given existing theories that trace injustice to culpable state and other institutional failures. I then develop a novel account of structural injustice, the Complexity View, that unravels this dilemma. The emergent properties of human actions in a complex society explain what is “structural” about structural injustice, specifically how it can arise without (culpable) wrongdoing. Structural injustice is unjust because it is wrong to contribute to social processes that cause harm and to passively accept preventable forms of vulnerability and deprivation as tragic misfortunes. But this account of structural injustice has a sobering implication: while complexity explains what distinguishes structural injustice from other wrongs, it also sets significant epistemic limits on social reform.

title: Marriage as Slavery: Oroonoko, the Slave Trade, and the Origins of English Feminism
abstract: This article investigates Mary Astell’s controversial comparison of marriage to slavery. While existing scholarship situates this analogy within the neo-Roman republican framework, which defined slavery as subjection to absolute rule, I investigate another paradigm: the transatlantic slave trade. To make this case, the article traces the influence of Aphra Behn’s Oroonoko (1688) on early feminist thought. By foregrounding the market logic underpinning chattel slavery, Behn popularized the idea that slavery’s harms were rooted, not in absolute power, but in the commodification of human beings. Astell appropriated this insight, showing that marriage resembled slavery not because husbands wielded power over wives but because the institution had been commodified: women were treated as things to be bought and sold. In uncovering this genealogy of feminist thought, the article highlights the enduring contributions of the “first” English feminists—insights that are entangled with, and shaped by, the development of the slave trade.

title: Democratic Accountability with Citizen Coproduction
authors: JIE MA, KEITH E. SCHNAKENBERG, IAN R. TURNER
abstract: Many policies require citizens to actively participate in their implementation in order to be successful, a situation referred to as citizen coproduction. Though citizen coproduction is necessary in many policy areas, it could create difficulties for democratic accountability because citizens and politicians share responsibility for policy failures and attribution of blame may be difficult. We analyze the problem of democratic accountability with citizen coproduction in the context of a model in which politicians, who vary with respect to their competence at selecting policies, choose whether to implement policies whose success depends on citizen coproduction choices. For citizens, the problem is one of attribution: when coproduction is low, it may be hard to select good incumbents because policy failures are frequent even when policy choices are good. Incumbents anticipate these effects, which sometimes implies that they are less likely to choose reforms when they are more likely to be successful.

title: What Would It Mean to Democratize Finance? An Evaluation of Divergent Conceptions of Democracy and Finance
abstract: Calls to “democratize finance” abound today. Yet this apparent consensus obscures sharply divergent conceptions of both democracy and finance. This article maps these demands along two axes, distinguishing between access- and power-based conceptions of democracy, and between three dimensions of finance: payment, capital markets, and banking. We then develop three normative claims. First, we argue that conceptions that reduce democratization to expanded market access are not merely insufficient but, when applied to speculative capital markets, amount to predatory inclusion. Second, thicker accounts of democratization as equal inclusion are normatively more promising but internally unstable, as their democratic commitments generate pressures toward power sharing. Third, the most plausible conceptions of democratizing finance are power-centered and involve greater public control over credit creation and allocation. Rather than defending a single institutional solution, the article assesses a range of reform proposals while specifying a normative threshold for evaluating what it would mean to democratize finance.

title: The Production of Inequality in High-Risk Pregnancy
abstract: How do socioeconomically advantaged individuals maintain their health advantage? Prior work shows how high socioeconomic status (SES) individuals secure advantages in areas such as housing or the labor market and provides longstanding evidence of health inequalities across SES. However, we have a more limited understanding of the mechanisms behind how high-SES individuals leverage structural advantage to improve their own health. This article draws on in-depth interviews with people diagnosed with gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), a high-risk pregnancy condition that requires an intensive treatment regimen over a short timeframe, to reveal how socioeconomic advantage translates into health advantage. Socioeconomic advantage creates inequalities in health through multiple pathways, including excess financial resources that can be used to acquire health-relevant resources and access to flexible time to dedicate toward strict GDM management. Socioeconomically advantaged participants can thus respond to a diagnosis with GDM more quickly and efficiently than can disadvantaged participants. The divergent approaches to managing GDM that I uncover support advantaged individuals’ hyper-compliance with treatment guidelines, what I call going “above and beyond,” that translate into qualitatively different interactions with healthcare professionals than those of low-SES individuals, compounding structural (dis)advantage. Explicating the mechanisms through which high-SES individuals maintain health advantage identifies new directions for studying the production of inequality.

title: When, Where, and Why Might Elected Political Elites Reach for Democratic Innovations?
authors: Şule Yaylacı, Mark Warren, Edana Beauvais
abstract: Electoral democracies are under strain. Elections and conventional relations of representation between elected politicians and citizens do not seem to be providing sufficient legitimacy for democratic governance. In principle, democratic innovations such as deliberative minipublics or participatory budgeting could supplement electoral systems so that they function more democratically. But elected representatives may resist these innovations due to unfamiliarity, perceived threats to their power, and the belief that traditional electoral methods suffice for democratic legitimacy. This paper theorizes the potential incentives for elected officials to adopt democratic innovations, examining the conditions under which innovations might align with their interests. Democratic deficits may, and often do, present electoral risks and challenges. By mapping democratic deficits onto elite incentives, we suggest when, where, and why the strategic motivations of elected officials might align with democratic innovations. We illustrate the theory with examples of democratic innovations drawn primarily from the Participedia database. We conclude that strategies for deepening democracy should include understanding how democratic innovations relate to incentives structured by electoral institutions, so that innovations might supplement rather than compete with electoral democracy.

title: Critical Ties: How NGOs Become Reliable Information Suppliers to International Organizations
authors: Florencia Montal, Gino Pauselli, María-José Urzúa
abstract: International organizations (IOs) monitor compliance with international norms but public criticism of member states remains discretionary. We argue that such criticism depends not only on mandates or political incentives, but on whether IOs can access information they deem credible. This credibility is socially produced. Through repeated interaction, IO staff develop trust in specific local non-governmental organizations (NGOs), which become reliable conduits of mandate-aligned and verifiable information. These trust-based ties reduce uncertainty and reputational risk, enabling public criticism. We test this argument using original data on press releases and NGO participation in public hearings at the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights from 1996 to 2020. Combining statistical analysis, an instrumental variable strategy, text analysis, and interview evidence, we show that the Commission is more likely to issue and to sharpen critical press releases when it has established ties with local NGOs focused on the relevant country and issue.

title: The Legacy of Mexico’s Drug War on Youth Political Attitudes
abstract: How does childhood exposure to large-scale criminal violence and militarized law enforcement shape political attitudes and behavior? We examine the case of Mexico’s drug war, where a generation has been raised amidst the country’s most violent conflict in over a century. Surveying nearly 3,000 urban youth to measure their political and interpersonal trust, we matched respondents to historical data on criminal violence and military confrontations and operations in their childhood municipalities. Disentangling the effects of criminal violence and military interventions, we find that exposure to homicidal violence during childhood erodes interpersonal trust and trust in law enforcement, while military interventions – especially those involving violent confrontations – broadly undermine trust in federal security institutions and generate political backlash against the parties that governed Mexico during the exposure period. These findings have important implications for young democracies affected by high crime and violence and advance our understanding of how criminal wars influence political socialization.

title: The Threshold Effect: Preference Falsification Versus Weak Preferences in Russian War Support
authors: Isabelle DeSisto, Grigore Pop-Eleches, Jacob R. Tucker
abstract: How reliable are surveys in autocracies? Using data from wartime Russia, we show why list experiments – commonly used to detect preference falsification – do not always reveal hidden dissent. We identify and test what we call the ‘threshold effect’: respondents may report support for a sensitive item in a direct question but omit it in a list experiment, not because they are lying, but because the list format can create a higher threshold for expressing support. We provide direct evidence of this effect and use two approaches to distinguish preference falsification from weak preferences. Both suggest that outright lying in Russia is limited, but many attitudes are weak and easily shaped by question framing. We conclude that while many Russians genuinely support the war against Ukraine, this support is shallow. Our findings suggest that researchers should take care when designing and interpreting survey questions that measure sensitive attitudes using indirect methods.

title: Recommendation Design: Can Mediators Implement Correlated Equilibria?
authors: Mikhail Anufriev, John Duffy, Valentyn Panchenko, Benjamin Young
abstract: We report results from a novel experiment studying individuals’ ability to act as mediators by designing incentive-compatible recommendation devices for rational robot agents, that is, to implement correlated equilibria. To test the skills required of a successful mediator, we vary both the games played by the agents and the mediator’s objective. Most participants successfully implement correlated equilibria across games, especially in games where coordination yields benefits. Across objectives, however, many participants initially favour fair and efficient devices, even when these properties are not incentivised, suggesting that fairness and efficiency serve as important heuristics in recommendation design.

title: Reconciling Aggregate And Firm-Level Tariff Pass-Through: Evidence From The 2018–2019 Us Tariffs On China
authors: Haichao Fan, Lixin Tang, Wei Tian, Caiyun Wu, Miaojie Yu
abstract: Research finds complete tariff pass-through at the product level during the 2018-2019 US-China trade war. Using firm-level customs data, we find a significant decrease in Chinese firms’ ex-tariff prices in response to US tariffs, which indicates incomplete pass-through. A one-percentage-point tariff increase reduces prices by 0.172 percentage points for the highest-priced 25% of exporters while having negligible effects on firms with below-median prices. US tariffs increase Chinese exporters’ probability of exiting the US market, with larger effects for lower-priced firms. The product-level complete pass-through results from two offsetting forces—price reduction by incumbents and market exits by lower-priced firms.

title: Do Water Audits Work?
authors: Jesper Akesson, Rajat Kochhar, Robert W Hahn, Robert D Metcalfe
abstract: Water suppliers are showing greater interest in using residential water audits to promote conservation. Yet there is limited causal evidence on their effectiveness, persistence, and welfare implications. We address this gap using a natural field experiment in the United Kingdom that randomly assigns about 45,000 households to receive different behavioural encouragements to complete an online home water audit. Our analysis yields three main findings. First, financial incentives substantially increase audit take-up and lead to large short-run reductions in water use: among compliers, consumption falls by about 17 per cent over a two-month period. The size of the incentive matters for participation but not for the magnitude of conservation. Second, conservation effects attenuate rapidly, becoming undetectable after roughly two months. As a result, the intervention yields small welfare gains, with per capita net benefits typically below Â£1 under a wide range of assumptions. Third, targeting high-use households roughly doubles short-run conservation effects but remains insufficient to generate sizable welfare gains because conservation does not persist. Overall, while audits and incentives induce meaningful short-run conservation, their policy value depends critically on whether these effects persist.

title: International Migration, Exchange Rate Shocks, and Education Investment
abstract: International migrants channel resources from abroad, but if they cause the state to reduce public investments back home, they may lead to negative development outcomes. I use Indonesian migrant returnees data and district variations in migration destinations and exchange rate shocks to estimate the effects of foreign income shocks on education investments. Households in higher-shock districts send more children to school, prompting the government to increase public schools. The state also provides other public goods complementing household investments. These responses to shocks are not driven by taxation or elections, but rather by administrative splitting that strengthens accountability channels.

title: Agrarian Origins of Individualism and Collectivism
authors: Martin Fiszbein, Yeonha Jung, Dietrich Vollrath
abstract: This study examines the influence of agricultural labour intensity on individualism across U.S. counties. We measure historical labour intensity in agriculture by combining data on crop-specific labour requirements with county-level crop mix around 1900. Potential endogeneity in agricultural labour intensity is addressed using climate-induced variation in crop mix. The estimates indicate that a one standard deviation increase in labour intensity is associated with a reduction of 0.2-0.3 standard deviations in individualism (as captured by the share of children with infrequent names). We also document significant changes in individualism over time, in relation to within-county shifts in labour intensity due to mechanisation and the boll weevil shock. Further evidence from contemporary online search queries and social media language suggests that historical labour intensity continues to influence geographic variation in individualism today. Lastly, our decomposition of labour intensity provides insights into the mechanisms underlying this cultural impact.

title: Migration and Race: Central and Eastern European Perspectives. By KasiaNarkowicz, AnnaGawlewicz and KonradPędziwiatr (eds.), London: Taylor and Francis, 2025. 158 pp. £116.00 (hardback). ISBN: 978‐1‐03‐251815‐2
Inoculating against fatalistic beliefs: a comparative test of narrative and non-narrative strategies
abstract: This study compares the effectiveness of narrative and non-narrative inoculation messages in reducing fatalistic beliefs and fostering resistance to conflicting cancer information. A two-phase randomized experiment (N = 572 in Phase 1; n = 332 in Phase 2) tested their effects on counterarguing against attack, cancer fatalism, perceived efficacy, and intentions to adopt cancer risk-reduction behaviors. Compared with control, both inoculation messages reduced cancer fatalism, enhanced perceived efficacy, and increased certain intentions to adopt certain risk-reduction behaviors. Narrative inoculation elicited more counterarguing against attack than the non-narrative counterpart. Inoculation effects also varied by baseline fatalism, functioning therapeutically by immediately reducing initially high fatalism and, more modestly, prophylactically by maintaining initially low fatalism. These findings extend inoculation theory by elucidating the role of message format in sustaining resistance to negative media effects, and by demonstrating the theory’s potential dual prophylactic–therapeutic functionality in a fatalistic belief context.

title: Crises and regime instability: autocratization and democratization pathways across political regimes
abstract: To what extent are political regimes vulnerable to crises? Established research has explored in depth how crises can compromise regime stability, from Linz's foundational studies to contemporary investigations. Yet, such contributions remain scattered across unconnected concepts, methods, and applications, thus hindering cumulative knowledge. This article crafts a coherent examination of different crises and their impacts on regime instability, with a twofold contribution: first, it synthesizes the findings of such a large literature; second, it advances them through a single framework and an extensive empirical test of their external validity. Applying various indicators of economic, violent, and disaster-related crises, our global study implements a broad range of time-series cross-sectional regression models on direct and moderated effects on different types of regime instability (alteration in democracy levels, democratic upturns/downturns, democratization/autocratization episodes, and democratic breakdown/transition) in democracies and autocracies. The findings not only confirm but also unveil multiple crises-related pathways of regime change, especially for economic and violent crises, and a generally greater fragility of autocracies compared to democracies, both in the face of the impact of a single crisis and in the occurrence of simultaneous crises. This reassessment bridges previous examinations, offers important policy suggestions, and opens up ways for further inquiries.

title: Securing support, avoiding harm? Civilian support, community organization, and rebel landmine use in Colombia
abstract: How do armed groups manage the trade-off between securing and accessing support from civilian populations and minimizing the risk of exposing them to violence? While rebels often depend on local communities, their proximity exposes civilians to significant risks. This article addresses this dilemma by examining the use of landmines by Colombian guerrilla groups. Although landmines are expected to offer an effective and low-cost means to offset asymmetries in civil wars, their indiscriminate nature threatens the very communities on which rebels rely. I argue that while rebels are more likely to lay minefields where they enjoy greater local support, they should also attempt to reduce risks to civilians in these areas, especially when faced with stronger resistance from local communities. Using cross-sectional, subnational data from Colombia's national mine action program, I show that guerrilla groups indeed laid more landmines in more supportive municipalities. However, while such support does not appear to correlate with restraint in landmine use, higher levels of community organization are associated with minefields being laid further from populated areas and with fewer civilian mine accidents. The findings contribute to research on civilian victimization, rebel governance, and restraint in wartime violence, with implications for mine clearance and civilian protection.

title: Guilty by association: patrons, purges, and promotions under personalism
abstract: Mounting scholarship grapples with the causes and consequences of power personalization in autocracies. Prominent research suggests that as the personalist dictator amasses power, he tends to repress potential rivals from his inner circle to stave off mortal threats to his rule. Because military supporters of fallen elites are considered especially menacing to the dictator, they should be more susceptible to a similar fate than other officers, but little empirical work systematically studies authoritarian purges of secondary targets in the military. Drawing on monthly data from 1955–1976 on the leaders of the regional commands of the People's Liberation Army, I find China's regional military leaders hailing from patronage networks of disgraced top civilian and military leaders at the center were more likely to be purged or otherwise experienced more adverse career outcomes than their counterparts without such tainted associations amidst the consolidation and culmination of Mao's personalist rule.

title: From aggrieved to activist: group grievances, personal resources, and participation repertoires
abstract: From voting to violence, politicized ethnicities shape many aspects of politics. Yet, within-group variation in how individuals respond to ethnic inequalities remains understudied. This article examines how perceived group grievance and personal resources combine to shape political participation repertoires. We argue that perceived group grievance can facilitate both conventional and contentious participation, but that individuals' repertoires are conditioned by socioeconomic status: Only the poorest and least educated should be willing to join contentious activities when protests entail risk of repression. Using 2016 survey data from Nepal collected during a period of high contention, we show that while middle class group members respond to perceived group grievance primarily with conventional political activities, such as party work and contacting politicians, individuals from the lowest socioeconomic strata are more likely to respond by supplementing or replacing conventional participation with protests and strikes. Additional analyses suggest that variation in civic skills, measured as literacy, basic political knowledge, and proficiency in the official language, provides the most likely explanation for these differences. The combination of within- and between-group inequalities is commonly seen to increase the risk of recruitment to armed groups. Our findings suggest that they can also serve as a catalyst for nonviolent contentious action. Moreover, the socioeconomic composition of identity groups could help condition the mode of their political struggle.

title: Classifying strategy use in multiattribute subjective choice: Application to conjoint experiments in political science
abstract: Conjoint experiments are extensively used across multiple disciplines to make inferences about preferences over multiattribute alternatives. Much previous research has analyzed the importance of attributes at the aggregate level. Here, we focus on understanding individual-level behavior and, specifically, on strategy use. We present a Bayesian cognitive model of strategy use that performs attribute weight inference (how important an attribute is), attribute level inference (which value of the attribute is favored), and latent-mixture inference to classify strategy use among well-established strategies in cognitive science. We then validate and apply our model to two conjoint experiments ( N = 3,762) focusing on three political domains (attitudes toward immigrants, political candidates, and climate policy). We find that the simplest heuristic strategy is the highest probability in all conditions and that approximately 67–76% of subjects are classified as using different strategies depending on the political domain. Our model additionally highlights how aggregate-level inference on the weight of an attribute can be meaningfully decomposed by individual differences in strategy use and preferences over attributes. In addition, our experiments include a set of experimental design manipulations that increase different dimensions of complexity and show their impact on strategy classification.

title: The economic returns to citizenship: Evidence from a meta-analysis
abstract: Citizenship is widely summarized as producing a “naturalization premium” for immigrants, but naturalization is selected: immigrants who naturalize differ in language, residence, employment, and motivation. We provide a quantitative meta-analysis of citizenship effects on immigrant earnings, synthesizing 60 preferred estimates from 31 studies. How a study separates the effect of citizenship from selection into citizenship—its identification strategy—explains more variation in estimates than destination country, citizenship regime, or any other study feature we code. Averaging published estimates with a multilevel random-effects model yields a pooled premium of 9.9% (95% CI 5.1 to 14.9), and 11.0% (95% CI 5.7 to 16.6) when pooling within study-country cells. But this average conceals sharp differences across research designs. The randomized encouragement study relying on a lottery to overcome selection implies a near-zero effect of 1.9% (95% CI −1.3 to 5.3); the regression-discontinuity study yields 11.3% (95% CI 5.2 to 17.8); estimates from policy reforms and within-unit panels are positive on average but too imprecise to distinguish from either zero or the pooled average; and observational instrumental-variable estimates average 53.0% (95% CI 27.6 to 83.5). Excluding observational instrumental-variable estimates reduces the pooled premium to 6.0% (95% CI 3.8 to 8.2). Reanalyzing the randomized trial data shows the same pattern: Experimental estimates are near zero, while an observational difference-in-differences comparison based on self-selected citizenship uptake implies a 9.6% gain (95% CI 4.0 to 15.5) four years post lottery, a bias standard pretrend tests do not detect. The published citizenship premium is positive, but its size and causal interpretation depend on research design.

title: Taxing the talent that builds American science
Can they agree on what to disagree about? Patterns of issue agenda setting in the 2020 US presidential election
abstract: American voters, politicians, and media are increasingly hostile toward out-partisans and frequently disagree about the content of policies. This development raises an even more fundamental question about the nature of politics in highly polarized societies: Can the political actors even agree on what issues to disagree about, and why? To answer this critical question, we generate a massive new dataset covering communication by key actors from the last 2 months of the 2020 US Presidential election, including the presidential candidates (all tweets by Donald Trump and Joe Biden), the main news organizations (CNN and Fox News), and a large and original voter survey (N ~ 24,000) with daily representative data. Surprisingly, we find that the patterns of agenda setting in the 2020 election reduced rather than fueled agenda diversity and that the major political actors generally agreed on what the most important issues were in this otherwise polarized election.

title: A Replication of “Your Money, Your Life, or Your Freedom? A Discrete Choice Experiment on Trade‐Offs During a Public Health Crisis”
authors: Binzizi Dong, Chung‐An Chen, Soojin Kim, Chih‐Wei Hsieh
abstract: A prior experiment conducted in Italy examined how individuals navigate trade‐offs among money, life, and freedom during government‐mandated lockdowns. This study replicates that experiment across three Confucian societies: Shanghai (China), Singapore, and Taipei (Taiwan). The findings indicate that, in the aggregate sample, the preference pattern of “money > life > freedom” mirrors that reported in the original study. However, when analyzed separately, residents of Taipei show stronger preferences for income and freedom than their counterparts in Singapore and Shanghai. Conversely, Singaporeans demonstrate heightened concern regarding the loss of life. In addition to replicating previous findings, this study contributes to the field of comparative public administration by highlighting the importance of considering contextual nuances in the formulation of crisis‐management practices by public managers.

title: The 150‐Year‐Old Hybrid Organization: A Historical View on Municipally Owned Corporations ( MOC ) in Sweden
abstract: This article presents a 150‐year longitudinal analysis of the development of municipally owned corporations (MOCs) in Sweden, tracing their emergence in the mid‐nineteenth century, their expansion during the growth of the welfare state, and their transformation in the era of market‐oriented public sector reform. While MOCs are commonly discussed in relation to New Public Management (NPM) and contemporary forms of hybrid governance, this perspective overlooks their much longer historical trajectory. Drawing on three major Swedish government inquiries (1924, 1965, and 1982), complemented by secondary historical sources, we examine how MOCs have evolved across changing political, economic, and administrative contexts. The article conceptualizes MOCs as constitutional hybrids, organizations that combine elements of public authority and corporate governance by design, and employs insights from institutional theory and historical institutionalism to analyze their long‐term development. The findings identify three historical phases characterized by changing functions, governance rationales, and institutional expectations. Across these periods, MOCs were repeatedly reinterpreted and adapted to new circumstances while maintaining their basic organizational form. The study contributes to the literature on hybridity by demonstrating that hybridity should be understood not merely as a contemporary consequence of public sector reform, but as a historically evolving institutional condition. We argue that the enduring presence of MOCs reflects the adaptive capacity of hybrid organizational forms, whose flexibility allows them to accommodate shifting demands for efficiency, legitimacy, accountability, and public value. By historicizing hybridity, the article offers a new perspective on institutional resilience, and the long‐term evolution of public governance.

title: Skills, Not Just Will: Experimental Evidence From Uganda on Transparency in Public Procurement
authors: Mark T. Buntaine, Alex Bagabo, Paul Bukuluki, Brigham Daniels, Gerald Padde Auku
abstract: Governments are usually the largest purchasers of goods and services, creating significant opportunities for corruption. We study whether offering training and technical assistance to procurement officials in 50 Ugandan districts prompted them to publish procurement actions on an online public portal, as legally required. Among districts that received the training and technical assistance program, we randomized whether procurement officials received information in advance about their eligibility to earn a public award for adherence to these transparency standards. We use national administrative data across multiple financial years and 134 district governments to evaluate impacts. The training and technical assistance program increased the number and value of procurement actions uploaded several‐fold, while award eligibility did not have similarly large effects. These results suggest that motivation problems may be overemphasized in the fight against corruption. Building capacity in accounting and transparency could provide effective guardrails against corruption.

title: Artificial Intelligence, Bureaucratic Discretion, and Democratic Administration
abstract: Since the start of the COVID ‐19 pandemic, many countries have been using artificial intelligence ( AI ) to replace civil service personnel. We argue that this practice undermines core democratic values. Using the public values framework, we identify four clusters of values that are threatened when bureaucratic discretion is transferred to algorithms: accountability, fairness and equity, individual consideration, and reason‐giving. Each of these values is incompatible with how algorithms render decisions. Because algorithms produce outputs based on statistical regularities, they diffuse responsibility across multiple parties, fail to make accurate predictions about anomalous cases, and attenuate citizens' claims to individualized consideration. Thus, this article frames AI adoption as a constitutional question about which decisions can be automated, and which should remain under human control because they implicate democratic values. We propose a centaur model in which AI supports rather than replaces human officials, which can preserve efficiency while protecting democratic governance.

title: Public Management of Deregulated Systems: Challenges and Opportunities in the Public Management of Retail Energy Markets
authors: Noah Dormady, Jenya Kahn‐Lang, Yiseon Choi, Yufan Ji, Samantha Fox, Alberto Lamadrid, Matthew Hoyt
abstract: Many critical infrastructure services operate within quasi‐regulated (i.e., “deregulated”) markets. Public managers face a unique set of challenges and opportunities in the administration and oversight of these markets. Administrative and regulatory challenges exist because public managers are required to balance an open and competitive marketplace while confronting multiple market failures (e.g., consumer inattention, imperfect competition) alongside organizational, management, and legal and regulatory enforcement challenges. There are real‐world consequences of administrative choices on economic (in)efficiency and consumer equity. This paper provides public managers with a comprehensive review of the public management challenges and opportunities associated with managing deregulated retail electricity markets. It then provides a review of empirical research and an empirical example for one category of these challenges—consumer equity. The paper concludes with a multi‐disciplinary discussion of the role of public managers in deregulated marketplaces and public policy options to address both equity and efficiency challenges.

title: Reply to Kettl: Beyond Bureaucracy: Why AI Demands a Fourth Way in Public Administration
abstract: Kettl argues public administration faces a crisis rooted in widening gaps between scholars and practitioners and between the field's core ideas and current governance issues. We identify a critical example: artificial intelligence (AI) adoption in government. AI fundamentally transforms public organizations, redistributing tasks and discretion between humans and algorithms, embedding instrumental rationality into administrative processes, and reconfiguring authority structures. These developments challenge three longstanding pillars of public administration: bureaucratic neutrality, the politics‐administration dichotomy, and democratic governance. We argue that any proposed “Fourth Way” must center democratic resilience and technological stewardship, incorporating algorithmic transparency requirements and participatory governance structures that preserve public—and especially democratic—values.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Policing and Perceived Legitimacy: Does Gender Representation Make a Difference?
abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly transforms public administration, understanding its impact on perceived legitimacy becomes paramount, particularly, in high‐stakes areas such as policing. While existing research offers mixed evidence on whether government AI use enhances or undermines citizens' perceptions of fairness and trust, the conditions moderating these effects remain underexplored. Drawing on representative bureaucracy theory, this study uses a survey experiment to investigate how gender representation moderates the effect of AI use on citizens' perceived fairness and trust in domestic violence units (DVUs). Results show that female representation positively moderates the legitimacy impact of a DVU's AI use; whereas AI use decreases female respondents' perceived fairness and trust in male‐dominated DVUs, these negative effects disappear in female‐dominated DVUs. Our findings identify representation as a key context shaping citizens' responses to government AI use, extending representative bureaucracy theory by demonstrating its indirect symbolic effects.

title: The Right‐Wing Idea Factory: From Traditionalism to Trumpism. By Donald F.Kettl, New York: Oxford University Press, 2026. 248 pp. (hardback). ISBN: 978‐0‐19‐777829‐6
Citizens' Expectations vs. Recruitment Signals: Are Public Administrations Trying to Attract the Ideal Public Servant?
abstract: Job advertisements play a crucial role in attracting applicants, yet little is known about how closely they reflect the values citizens expect from public servants. Drawing on signaling theory and prior research on citizens' normative expectations of ideal public servants, this study employs a large language model to analyze 1825 job advertisements from health and transportation departments across seven U.S. states. Compared to the values citizens associate with ideal public servants in previous research, job advertisements predominantly emphasize values, such as expertise and dedication, while undersignaling relational values like serviceability, responsiveness, and honesty. Our findings suggest a misalignment between the values signaled in recruitment practices and those citizens associate with the ideal public servant. By adopting a citizen‐driven perspective, this study prompts scholars and public managers to question recruitment practices that may underemphasize values citizens prioritize in public servants, potentially limiting public administrations' ability to attract qualified candidates.

title: Reply to Kettl: Great Workplaces, Public Employee Legitimacy and the Fourth Way
abstract: In Public Administration and the Crisis of American Democracy, Don Kettl asks why some federal agencies are great places to work while others are not, pointing to the persistent gap between NASA and the Department of Homeland Security. This essay argues that the answer may turn on how the legitimate role of public employees in democratic governance is construed. Drawing on three interpretive frames—bureaucracy, democracy, and pragmatism—it examines 2024 employee survey responses at NASA and DHS that map onto these frames. DHS appears dominated by the bureaucracy frame, positioning employees as implementers whose voice is risky and expertise underused. NASA blends all three frames, treating employees as contributors, stewards, and problem solvers. These frames offer a partial explanation for Kettl's puzzle and a conceptual tool for his “fourth way”: great government workplaces are built when public servants are recognized as legitimate contributors to democratic governance, not just cogs in a bureaucratic wheel.

title: How Does Wage Inequality Affect the Labor Movement?
authors: Barbara Biasi, Zoë Cullen, Julia Gilman, Nina Roussille
abstract: This paper provides evidence on how wage inequality among workers affects the labor movement using three complementary research designs: a vignette experiment with union organizers, a natural policy experiment that increased wage inequality among Wisconsin school teachers, and an information intervention during the 2023 Writers Guild of America strike. Across all studies, we find that inequality undermines union strength through multiple channels. First, workers with high individual bargaining power are more likely to withdraw support in unequal environments, preferring individual over collective bargaining. Second, union organizers facing hypothetical choices strategically respond to inequality in ways that may preserve membership but limit redistribution, such as shifting their campaign away from wages and choosing smaller, more homogeneous bargaining units.

title: BUSING TO OPPORTUNITY? THE IMPACTS OF THE METCO VOLUNTARY SCHOOL DESEGREGATION PROGRAM ON URBAN STUDENTS OF COLOR
abstract: School assignment policies are a key lever for expanding access to high-performing schools and promoting racial and socioeconomic integration. For over 50 years, the Metropolitan Council for Educational Opportunity (METCO) has bussed students of color from Boston, Massachusetts, to relatively wealthier and predominantly white suburbs. I estimate the effects of attending a high-performing suburban school by comparing applicants who receive enrollment offers with applicants who do not. A two-stage least squares approach exploits waitlist assignment priorities and controls for a rich set of characteristics from birth records and application data. Attending a suburban school boosts math and English test scores, reduces dropout, and increases on-time high school graduation. Four-year college aspirations, enrollment, and graduation increase along with earnings in adulthood. Students whose parents did not attend college and boys experience the largest effects. The evidence points to several mechanisms, including access to higher value-added schools, higher-achieving peers, and schools with stronger college-going norms. Participants are more likely to be tracked into lower-performing classes, implying that effects could be larger with access to more advanced coursework. District value-added estimates suggest that students’ educational trajectories shift at least as much as they would from growing up in the suburban districts.

title: The Origin of Risk
authors: Alexandr Kopytov, Mathieu Taschereau-Dumouchel, Zebang Xu
abstract: We propose a tractable model in which risk, at both the micro and macro levels, is endogenous and driven by incentives. In the model, each firm chooses the mean and the variance of its productivity process, as well as how it covaries with the productivity of other firms. Aggregate risk arises when firms select productivity processes that are correlated with one another. The theory predicts that larger firms and those with lower markups are less volatile and less correlated with aggregate productivity. We find support for these predictions in the data. Through their impact on risk-taking decisions, distortions such as taxes and markups can make GDP more volatile in equilibrium. In a calibrated version of the model, removing distortions significantly reduces GDP volatility.

title: Retrieval Failures and Consumption Smoothing: A Field Experiment on Seasonal Poverty
authors: Ned Augenblick, B Kelsey Jack, Supreet Kaur, Felix Masiye, Nicholas Swanson
abstract: People may fail to recall and use information they already know when making decisions. We empirically investigate whether such “retrieval failures” distort consumption-smoothing behavior among Zambian farmers, who derive their income from one annual harvest and spend it over the course of the year. We document that individuals underestimate upcoming spending by 50%, creating scope for undersaving. To improve recall, we randomize an intervention that prompts people to think through their future expenses associatively in categories—without providing any external information or guidance. Treated individuals increase “remembered” expenses by 36%–60%; as predicted by the memory literature, effects are concentrated among small, irregular, and stochastic items. Immediate spending drops and, six weeks after the intervention, treated households hold 15% higher savings. They subsequently enter the hungry season—the final months of the year when consumption typically declines sharply—with one additional month of savings, leading to a flatter spending profile over the year. Households use the increased savings to self-finance additional farm investment, resulting in a 9% increase in the next year’s crop revenue. We replicate the intervention’s effect on beliefs among low-income Americans, suggesting that retrieval failures generalize across settings and populations.

title: Monetary Policy Invariance, Hysteresis, and Optimal Inflation
authors: Mirko Abbritti, Agostino Consolo, Sebastian Weber
abstract: Standard New Keynesian (NK) models feature an optimal inflation target well below 2%, limited welfare losses from business cycle fluctuations and long-term monetary neutrality. We develop an NK framework with endogenous productivity and downward nominal wage rigidity (DNWR) which challenges these results. The interaction between endogenous growth and DNWR generates asymmetric hysteresis effects on unemployment and R&D. As a consequence, the model features a nonvertical long-run Phillips curve and a trade-off between price distortions and output hysteresis that changes the welfare-maximizing inflation rate to above 2%. Deviations from the optimal target carry welfare costs multiple times those in traditional NK models. Taylor rules that respond to the unemployment rate address more effectively the asymmetric hysteresis in our model. Results are robust to the inclusion of the effective lower bound on interest rates.

title: Neighborhood change and Black-White segregation: 2000–2020
abstract: This study examines the relationship between neighborhood racial change and metropolitan segregation in 2000–2020. The most surprising finding is that the principal source of declining Black-White segregation has not been Black growth in White neighborhoods. Instead, it is a phenomenon that has not been noticed up to now—a substantial Black exodus from Black neighborhoods. The same kinds of neighborhoods where Black newcomers were increasingly concentrated in older, poorer sections of central cities in the 1920–1970 decades are now hollowing out, as residents find new opportunities elsewhere. We show that White exit from predominantly White neighborhoods is also an important source of segregation decline. At the same time, however, many predominantly Black neighborhoods have growing Black populations, pushing segregation upwards. This pattern was described as “succession” in early studies of central cities, but it is now likely to be found in suburban neighborhoods with newer housing, a smaller Black population share, and higher socioeconomic status compared to other Black neighborhoods. These and other findings shed new light on why segregation is declining and also why it is so persistent.

title: Review of “Privileged Brotherhoods: Becoming Men at Elite All-Boys Schools”
Review of “Island Time: Theory Groups and the Social Production of Scientific Knowledge”
On legacy persistence: historical KKK organizations and racial exclusion in American sundown towns
authors: Kunyuan Qiao, Ashley V Reichelmann, Matthew O Hunt
abstract: Why do some communities perpetuate historical patterns of racial exclusion while others abandon them? We examine American sundown towns, communities that from the 1890s through the 1960s barred people of color from remaining within their borders after sunset. We argue that Second Wave Ku Klux Klan (KKK) organizations, active from 1915 through the 1940s, institutionalized and enforced this exclusion, embedding it in local structures. These structures imprinted White adolescents with negative racial attitudes toward Black people, and imprinted individuals subsequently engaged in residential sorting, remaining in or relocating to sundown towns with a strong KKK presence while avoiding those without such a history. Second Wave Klan prevalence therefore predicts the racial attitudes of White residents in historical sundown towns today. We find support for our hypotheses in a sample of more than 600 White respondents surveyed in historical sundown towns. We advance research on place-based racial legacies by showing that historical organized enforcement helps explain why legacies persist unevenly across communities and that this persistence operates through two individual-level mechanisms: attitudinal imprinting and residential sorting.

title: Life and debt in rural America
abstract: Sociology’s growing focus on household debt and wealth has overlooked a potentially salient axis of inequality: rural–urban disparities in the United States. Key facets of rural life indicate a disadvantage (e.g., higher poverty rates, lack of mainstream financial institutions) and a simultaneous advantage (e.g., predominantly White populations, lower cost of living). To address evidence gaps on rural–urban disparities in debt and wealth, we use Consumer Expenditure Survey data to (1) estimate rural–urban disparities in multiple kinds of household debt and wealth, (2) examine what may be driving these disparities, and (3) assess whether these disparities also vary by race. Our findings show that place is an important axis of US financial inequality. Compared to urban households, rural households consistently have less credit card, student loan, and mortgage principal debt, but they also have less retirement and liquid savings, and their homes are worth less. These differences largely persist above controls, suggesting that rurality shapes financial outcomes in ways not fully explained by income dynamics and population composition. Racial variations in debt and wealth are also pronounced within rural areas, mirroring national patterns. We offer careful interpretations of our findings in order to gauge the financial and material wellbeing of rural households, which is needed in a time of growing rural–urban economic and social divides.

title: Generational imprinting: how political events shape cohorts
abstract: Contemporary narratives of generational politics propose that formative experiences produce shared political opinions across an age cohort. In this article, I advance a theory of cohortization to challenge that view, arguing that large–scale political events produce differentiation within cohorts as much as differentiation between them. I investigate the implications of this framework through the killing of George Floyd and the subsequent Black Lives Matter protests in 2020, analyzing attitudes toward law enforcement among non-Hispanic White Americans from 2016 to 2024. Using survey data from Cooperative Congressional Election Study, American National Election Study, and the Nationscape, I show that younger and older cohorts diverged after the event, but this differentiation was driven exclusively by young Democrats and Independents. The end result was not a unified generation, but one internally divided along party lines. This finding qualifies theories of generational politics, emphasizing that formative experiences may intensify existing political divisions within cohorts.

title: A Replication Framework for Observational Research: From Specification Restriction to Specification Expansion
authors: Jonathan Ben-Menachem, Ari Galper, Nic Fishman
abstract: Sociology has remained relatively insulated from debates about the “replication crisis.” Heeding calls to consider replication more deeply, we introduce a distinction between two types of research reforms that have emerged in the wake of the crisis: specification-restricting and specification-expanding reforms. Specification restriction is often promoted as a way to increase the repeatability of research findings by controlling false positives. We argue that this statistical justification is less compelling in observational contexts—where the assumptions licensing false-positive control are harder to sustain and rigid ex ante analytical commitments can instead enshrine fragile specifications—than in experimental contexts. We further argue that apparently low replication rates do not necessarily imply a high prevalence of false positive findings. Instead, we propose a replication framework centered on specification-expanding reforms, stronger incentives for confirmatory research, and meta-analysis. This approach equips sociologists to assess the repeatability of findings and build a more cumulative discipline.

title: The Cognitive Housework Inventory: Developing Survey Questions to Measure the Division of Cognitive Housework
abstract: Housework is unequally shared in different-gender couples, leading to negative consequences for women and lowering couples’ relationship quality. Although qualitative research identifies cognitive housework as an important type of household labor, we lack validated measures of cognitive housework to use in survey settings, barring quantitative research on its division in broader populations and its effects on household members. We use an open-ended survey and cognitive interviews to develop the Cognitive Housework Inventory (CHI), a seven-item survey instrument to measure the division of cognitive housework among partnered individuals. We then validate the CHI using data from an online survey, along with pairwise correlations, exploratory factor analysis, and bivariate analyses by gender. Regression analyses estimating its associations with stress, burnout, and relationship satisfaction demonstrate how to use the CHI in empirical settings. Results indicate the CHI is a valid and parsimonious instrument that can be incorporated into larger surveys to ultimately generate additional quantitative data on the distribution of housework.

title: Dynamics of Local Clustering in Temporal Social Networks
authors: Cheng Wang, Omar Lizardo, David S. Hachen
abstract: While the local clustering coefficient is central to network analysis, it is typically treated as a static property. We introduce delta clustering to quantify changes in an individual's local clustering across adjacent time points in undirected networks. To address structural constraints, we develop a density-based decomposition expressing clustering as a weighted combination of subgraph-specific densities, clarifying how ego-network size and composition bound clustering change. We identify six triadic components distinguishing reconfiguration among persisting contacts from the integration and loss of ties. Using high-resolution university communication networks, we estimate fixed effects models accounting for network size interactions. Variation in delta clustering is driven primarily by density changes among persisting contacts, followed by the integration of new contacts, with magnitudes conditioned by ego-network size and baseline density. We further demonstrate the measure's explanatory power by linking daily clustering changes to individual behavioral outcomes. These results establish delta clustering as a size-aware, temporally grounded measure of local structural change in dynamic social networks.

title: How Model Choice and Memory Shape Preference Consistency in Large Language Models
abstract: When a language model answers a sequence of questions, researchers report the model and temperature but rarely what or how it was told about its own earlier answers. I show that this underreported setting behaves as a mode effect. Testing four large language model (LLM) families with revealed preference theory (GARP) across moral, economic, and social tasks ( N = 5,926 ), I find that how prior choices re-enter the prompt, the memory condition , moves the share of internally consistent subjects by up to 48 percentage points, mostly where that share starts lowest. Memory also influences which preferences the models express and, in a silicon-sampling extension, it brings the answers closer to the human distribution. Nonetheless, gains in consistency and surface fidelity do not necessarily translate into representativeness: a consistent, human-looking model may not represent any human population. For LLMs as social-science instruments, this study offers promise, caution, and a method for testing the stability of sequential outputs.

title: Prediction-Based Adaptive Designs for Reducing Wave Nonresponse Rates and Bias in Panel Surveys
authors: John Collins, Saskia Bartholomäus, Tobias Gummer, Bernd Weiß, Christoph Kern
abstract: Machine learning (ML)-based nonresponse prediction in panel surveys enables selective interventions. However, the optimal use of ML predictions in Adaptive Survey Design (ASD) remains uncertain. We propose a method that integrates field experiment results on incentives, questionnaire length, and questionnaire content with ML-based propensity models to simulate ASD strategies ex-post with minimal assumptions. Using German panel data, we show that treating 15 percent of panelists, selected through ML-based predictions and R-indicator analysis, with increased cash incentives or a survey module on the respondents’ preferred topic can reduce nonresponse rates by up to 2 percentage points. These strategies also reduced bias in selected variables. We present our method as a framework for survey researchers to evaluate the expected outcomes of multiple ASD regimes simultaneously in a realistic setting. The framework helps identify both the criteria for allocating treatments to specific participant groups and the most effective modifications to the survey protocol.

title: When Can We Use Two-Way Fixed Effects (TWFE)? A Comparison of TWFE and Novel Dynamic Difference-in-Differences Estimators
abstract: The conventional two-way fixed effects (TWFE) estimator has come under increasing scrutiny in settings with staggered treatment adoption. Recent research shows that TWFE can be biased when treatment effects vary across time or groups, prompting the development of several alternative dynamic difference-in-differences (DiD) estimators. Yet for applied researchers, it often remains unclear when TWFE is biased, what the newer estimators solve, and what limitations they all have. The authors provide an accessible overview of this literature and compare conventional TWFE with five dynamic DiD estimators using Monte Carlo simulations. The simulations consider realistic scenarios with time- and group-varying treatment effects, anticipation effects, and violations of parallel trends. The results show that much of the bias in TWFE reflects functional-form misspecification: when treatment effects are modeled in event time, TWFE performs well under time heterogeneity, with only modest bias in later posttreatment periods when strong group-specific heterogeneity is present. None of the new estimators is universally superior, and all involve trade-offs, with some being more robust to anticipation effects and others less sensitive to deviations from parallel trends. The authors illustrate these findings in an application on the motherhood earnings penalty using UK panel data, in which the dynamic treatment profiles are broadly similar across estimators despite some differences in long-run effects. The authors conclude that applied researchers should carefully consider potential effect heterogeneity and model it appropriately, whatever estimator they use. The authors also challenge the presumption that TWFE should invariably be abandoned in favor of newer DiD estimators.

title: Book Review: Democracy and Beauty: The Political Aesthetics of W.E.B. Du Bois , by Robert Gooding-Williams Democracy and Beauty: The Political Aesthetics of W.E.B. Du Bois, by Gooding-WilliamsRobert, New York, NY: Columbia University Press, 2025, 272 pp.
A Habit-Building View of Democracy: Mary Parker Follett and Motor Activities
abstract: Citizens of democracies should live democratic lives and develop democratic habits. That is one of Mary Parker Follett’s core insights on democracy. A child of the Gilded Age, Follett experienced the erosion of communal relationships, the intensification of socio-economic inequalities, and the alienation of ordinary people from the complex political system that governed their lives. She saw democracy become remote and foreign to citizens who had little control over what happened to them. Her solution was simple: to reinject a dose of democracy into the everyday life of citizens. This paper retrieves Follett’s embodied and habitual vision of democracy for contemporary political theory. Follett claimed that citizens should participate actively in the democratic life of their society; however, she conceived of democratic participation as going beyond decision-making and deliberative activities. She thought that participation in simple forms of embodied joint actions, like recreation and collective chores, could also benefit democracy. Drawing from Follett, I argue that participation in a wide variety of embodied practices of collective action provides benefits to individuals and society by instilling democratic habits in citizens. Those habits incline those who develop them to enter and maintain relationships as free and equal peers with all sorts of people to reach common ends. When faced with collective problems, therefore, these individuals are more likely to choose democratic collective action and to do so more effectively.

title: The Perils of Improvement: Burke, Slavery, and Colonial Governance in the West Indies
abstract: Edmund Burke’s thoughts on plantation slavery have long been the subject of scholarly attention. Too often, however, discerning Burke’s long-term intention in relation to slavery has taken precedence over examining the specific administrative strategies he proposed for managing enslaved populations in the interim. Seeking to remedy this gap, the article reads Burke’s Sketch for a Negro Code as an exercise in colonial ameliorationism; that is, a reform programme that looked to ameliorate the institution of slavery as a way of strengthening British colonialism in the West Indies and civilising the African coast. Using colonial ameliorationism as an interpretive lens, I argue, allows us to reconstruct a consistent Burkean vision for colonial management in the West Indies, one that survived his vacillations on the question of abolition. It also throws into doubt the common argument that Burke saw imperial governance in negative terms; a matter of taming abuses of power and exercising restraint. In the West Indies, by contrast, Burke’s commitment to ameliorationism led him to embrace a productive form of colonial power aimed at enhancing the physical and mental capacities of the enslaved population through discipline, religious instruction, and the encouragement of biological reproduction. I conclude by showing how Burke’s faith in the improvability of the slave system is vulnerable to his own criticisms of other projects for political reform; namely that a certain guilelessness can blind reformers to the dangers inherent in their projects and reconcile them to what they purport to oppose.

Predicting Irritation Disclosures in Romantic Relationships: Testing and Extending the Revelation Risk Model
authors: Rudy C. Pett, Anita L. Vangelisti
abstract: Feelings of irritation often emerge in romantic relationships. However, the theoretical mechanisms predicting whether individuals disclose these feelings to their romantic partner remain limited and largely reliant on examining indicators of future behavior rather than actual future behavior. Using a two-month, longitudinal survey design involving 448 participants, the current study tested the Revelation Risk Model (RRM) as a mechanism for predicting whether individuals would disclose or conceal feelings of irritation about their romantic partner. Relationship power was also incorporated as an additional predictor. The original RRM components (i.e., closeness, risk, communication efficacy, willingness to disclose) collectively predicted whether individuals disclosed or concealed feelings of irritation about their romantic partner. Relationship power predicted individuals’ communication efficacy, as well as perceived risk associated with disclosing their feelings of irritation. The findings are discussed in terms of their contributions to existing research on disclosure, irritations, and power in romantic relationships.

title: Media Use for Strong and Weak Ties: A Configural Examination of Personal Media System and Well-Being
authors: Ceciley X. Zhang, Ronald E. Rice
abstract: Taking a configural approach to personal media use, this study examined how strong- and weak-tie media configuration relate to digital stress and well-being. Using a sample of 1,197 U.S. adults (analytic N = 1,143), we explored how media configuration attributes (size, density, and centralization by tie strength, and homogeneity) are associated with well-being, directly and indirectly through five dimensions of digital stress (overconnectivity, communication overload, deficient self-regulation, self-presentation pressure, and technological frustration). Our results highlight the importance of maintaining a larger, more interconnected, and centralized weak-tie configuration, and overall, a more uniform configuration, for well-being benefits (direct and indirect). Notably, larger weak-tie configuration is indirectly associated with lower well-being through greater technological frustration, while larger strong-tie configuration is indirectly associated with higher well-being through lower technological frustration. These findings emphasize the relational context of communication media use and suggest tie-specific strategies for managing communication flows and supporting well-being.

title: From Hate Speech to Collective Action Intentions: The Role of Counter-Speech and Accuracy Cues Among Targeted Minorities
authors: Desiree Schmuck, Magdalena Obermaier, Nancy Molina-Rogers, Muniba Saleem
abstract: Online hate speech targeting minority groups poses a significant social identity threat to those affected, often prompting coping strategies like out-group avoidance or derogation, which can harm intergroup relations in diverse societies. However, collective action as an empowering response has received limited attention in this context. Drawing on the social identity model of collective action (SIMCA), this study examines both the mechanisms and boundary conditions of online hate speech’s impact on minority groups. Across two experiments ( N Study1 = 328 Muslims; N Study2 = 583 Latinos), we find that online hate speech increases group-based injustice, which in turn drives collective action intentions, supporting the SIMCA. This effect is amplified when information embedded in the online hate speech is perceived as inaccurate or flagged for inaccuracy. In Study 2, we further demonstrate that counter-speech can reduce group-based injustice and, when paired with low-accuracy hate speech, enhance collective efficacy beliefs.

title: Early Access to Regular Employment and Long‐Term Immigrant Integration: Evidence from an Italian Amnesty Program
authors: Chiara Pronzato, Luca Mo Costabella, Simona Fiore
abstract: The early stages after arrival may play a crucial role in shaping immigrants’ long‐term integration trajectories. In this paper, we estimate the impact of obtaining regular employment within one year of arriving in Italy on the long‐term integration of immigrant individuals, approximately 10 years after arrival. A strong start in the host country is likely to play an important role in shaping long‐term integration outcomes and, ultimately, social cohesion. Despite a large literature on immigrant regularization, limited evidence exists on the causal impact of early access to regular employment on immigrants' long‐term social integration beyond labor market outcomes. To address this gap, we analyze a sample of immigrants from the Italian National Institute of Statistics (ISTAT) Social Condition and Integration of Foreign Citizens survey conducted in Italy in 2011–2012. Our impact estimates rely on an instrumental variable approach, leveraging a 2002 amnesty that increased the probability of obtaining a regular job depending on the time of arrival. We find that early engagement in regular employment has beneficial effects on various integration indicators, including trust in institutions, language proficiency, and cultural assimilation.
