title: Skin Tone as a Visual Cue in Political Campaigns: Evidence from Elections in Mexico
abstract: Research has long established that physical appearance and phenotypical traits influence how people evaluate political candidates. Skin color is one of the visual cues the electorate perceives during campaigns and media coverage, and a possible source of prejudice and bias. Here we use computational visual analysis to investigate the association between skin tone and electoral success during the 2024 Mexican Federal Elections. Our analyses incorporate important correlates not considered in prior research, most prominently news coverage, political ads, and social media use. We also account for geographic differences in average skin tone, explicitly modeling a source of variation that is obscured when skin tone is analyzed disregarding contextual baselines. We use fixed effects generalized linear models to control for state and party variation as well as candidate-level demographics, political experience, incumbency status, and media presence (news coverage, political ads, and social media use). Consistent with past work, we find that as candidates’ skin tone becomes darker, their predicted vote share declines. However, news coverage, political ads, and social media use are, together, more important predictors of electoral success than skin tone, indicating that this phenotypical trait is not as prominent a visual cue as earlier research suggested.

title: The Long-Term Effects of Cash Assistance
abstract: We investigate the long-term effects of cash assistance on beneficiaries and their children among participants in the Seattle-Denver Income Maintenance Experiment. Treated families in this randomized experiment received thousands of dollars in extra government benefits for three or five years in the 1970s. We match experimental records to Social Security Administration data using a novel algorithm, finding that treatment decreased adults' postexperimental annual earnings by $1,800 and increased their disability benefit applications. Effects were strongest around retirement age; evidence suggests possible occupational mechanisms. In contrast, children experienced no significant effects on earnings or interaction with the disability system. (JEL G51, H55, H75, I32, I38, J12, J14)

title: Who Gets a Family? The Consequences of Family and Congregate Care Allocation for Child Outcomes
abstract: Hundreds of thousands of children grow up in the US foster care system every year and are at high risk of experiencing negative outcomes such as incarceration and homelessness. This paper documents how the placement of foster children into families rather than congregate care improves their outcomes, using the exits of other children from families as an instrument for their placement setting. Policies that change which children are matched to families can achieve a large percentage of the gains from policies that add families to the foster care system due to heterogeneity in treatment effects. (JEL J12, J13, J18, K42)

title: Who Profits from Amateurism? Rent Sharing in Modern College Sports
authors: Craig Garthwaite, Nicole Holz, Jordan Keener, Matthew Notowidigdo
abstract: Intercollegiate amateur athletics in the United States have historically prevented student-athletes from receiving market wages, creating substantial economic rents that are primarily generated by men's football and basketball programs. Using financial data from college athletic departments, we estimate rent-sharing elasticities to measure how rents flow to women's sports and other men's sports and lead to increased spending on athletic facilities and coaches' salaries. Using player-level data, we find that the rent-sharing transfers spending away from students who are more likely to be Black and come from poor neighborhoods toward students more likely to be White and come from higher-income neighborhoods. (JEL I23, J15, J16, J31, L83, Z21, Z22)

title: Early Grade Retention Harms Adult Earnings
abstract: This paper provides new causal evidence on the effects of grade retention on educational attainment, behavioral outcomes, and labor market performance by analyzing Texas's reading test–based retention policy. Using a fuzzy regression discontinuity design, I find that third-grade retention significantly reduces annual earnings at age 26 by $3,477 (19 percent). While temporarily improving test scores, retention increases absenteeism, violent behavior, and juvenile crime, and reduces the likelihood of high school graduation. Moreover, retained students exhibit higher community college enrollment but lower public university attendance, though neither estimate is statistically significant. (JEL D91, H75, I21, I26, I28, J31)

title: Detection of Collusive Networks in Multistage Auctions
authors: Bruno Baránek, Leon Musolff, Vítězslav Titl
abstract: We develop a method for detecting cartels in multistage auctions. Our approach allows firms to act collusively against cartel members yet competitively otherwise. In these auctions, bidders submit initial bids and can later revise them downward. As initial bids are shaded, close initial bids indicate similar costs and thus create strong incentives to undercut rivals. We classify firm pairs as collusive if they ignore this incentive by failing to update bids against each other, relative to other pairs with similarly close initial bids. Our algorithm predicts Ukraine's Antimonopoly Committee sanctions: Classified pairs are nine times more likely to be sanctioned. (JEL D22, D44, H57, K21, L12, P31, P35)

title: From Access to Achievement: The Primary School-Age Impacts of an At-Scale Preschool Construction Program in Highly Deprived Communities
authors: Marina Bassi, Bruno Besbas, Lelys Dinarte-Diaz, Saravana Ravindran, Ana Reynoso
abstract: We evaluate a large-scale public preschool construction program in deprived rural communities in Mozambique using a randomized controlled trial. The program increased preschool enrollment from 2 to 75 percent, improved primary school enrollment and progression, and led treated children to score higher in cognitive and social-emotional skills tests. Impacts were strongest among children of illiterate parents, in less poor households, and living near preschools. We provide evidence that preschool construction mediates later educational success at primary school age. We also detect increased parental investment in children and higher preschool enrollment for younger siblings. Finally, we estimate the program was implemented cost-effectively. (JEL I21, I26, I32, J13, O15, O18)

title: All Roads Lead to Rome: Global Air Connectivity and Bilateral Trade
authors: Zheng Wang, Feicheng Wang, Zhuo Zhou
abstract: Using itinerary-level global air traffic data, this paper proposes a novel instrumental variable to estimate the effect of in-person interactions on bilateral trade. By exploiting exogenous variations in air connectivity that are driven by third-country connecting capacities, we show that increased air connections boost trade, especially for complex industries and new products. Online interactions appear to be a limited substitute for in-person contact. These findings confirm the role of in-person communications in reducing information-sharing barriers. Our estimation approach also provides a useful tool for evaluating the social and economic impacts of a complex transport network. (JEL D83, F14, L93, R41)

title: Money, Time, and Grant Design
abstract: We conduct survey experiments to test how the design of scientific grants—the money and time awarded—can be used to manage researchers. On average, researchers are relatively unwilling to trade off money for time when choosing among grants. However, there is significant heterogeneity in researchers' preferences. Conditional on receiving a grant, different designs cause only minor changes in researchers' plans for how they would use the funding. Marginal changes in grant design are more relevant for selection effects (funders' ability to attract certain researchers) than treatment effects (funders' ability to change researchers' strategies). (JEL C83, I23, O31)

title: Designing Incentives for Impatient People: An RCT Promoting Exercise to Manage Diabetes
authors: Shilpa Aggarwal, Rebecca Dizon-Ross, Ariel Zucker
abstract: Many people are impatient. We introduce domain-specific discounting to a contracting model and test a strategy for improving incentives when people are impatient over effort: implement time-bundled contracts that make the payment for future effort increase in current effort. Using a randomized evaluation of an exercise incentive program among diabetics in India, we find that time-bundled contracts generate equivalent effort to time-separable contracts at 15 percent lower cost. Moreover, they perform 30 percent better among individuals with above-median effort impatience. Pooled across contracts, incentives increase steps by 20 percent and improve blood sugar relative to a control group. (JEL D86, D91, I12, I18, O12)

title: Do Workfare Programs Live Up to Their Promises? Experimental Evidence from Côte d'Ivoire
authors: Marianne Bertrand, Bruno Crépon, Alicia Marguerie, Patrick Premand
abstract: We study contemporaneous and post-program impacts of a public works program which provides urban youth seven months of employment at the formal minimum wage with complementary training in entrepreneurship or job search. During the program, the employment rate only increases slightly, but we find a shift toward wage jobs, higher earnings and savings, as well as positive changes in work habits, behaviors, and well-being. After the program, we find no lasting impact on employment or behaviors, with only limited gains in earnings stemming from independent activities. Using machine learning to analyze heterogeneity, we show that alternative targeting approaches can substantially improve welfare. (JEL C45, G51, H53, I38, J13, J64, O15)

title: Globalization, Capital Taxation, and Development: Evidence from a Macrohistorical Database
authors: Pierre Bachas, Matthew Fisher-Post, Anders Jensen, Gabriel Zucman
abstract: This paper builds and analyzes a new global macrohistorical database of effective tax rates on capital and labor in 154 countries. We establish a new stylized fact: While effective capital tax rates fell in developed countries between 1965 and 2018, they rose in developing countries after 1990. Multiple country-, sector-, and firm-level research designs suggest that trade openness contributed to this rise by increasing the share of output produced in corporations and larger firms, where effective capital taxation is higher. In contrast to a common view, globalization appears in many countries to have supported governments' ability to tax capital. (JEL F41, F62, H24, H25, O19, O23)

title: Disastrous Displacement: The Long-Run Impacts of Landslides
abstract: Natural disasters displace millions of people a year, but their economic impacts are difficult to study when the affected population becomes dispersed. This paper estimates the long-run impacts of six landslides in Uganda on nearly the full affected population. The analysis exploits the sharp boundaries between households residing along a landslide path and those on the same slopes but outside the path. Years after the landslides, affected households earn 50 percent less income and are 18 percentage points less likely to report being satisfied with their lives. Further analysis points to social capital as a determinant of successful post-disaster recovery. (JEL H84, J11, O12, O13, Q54, R23, Z13)

title: Innovation through Inventor Mobility: Evidence from Noncompete Agreements
abstract: Proponents of labor mobility restrictions argue that innovation incentives more than offset harm to workers. Yet the causal effect of such policies on innovation is an open empirical question. Leveraging plausibly exogenous state-level changes in the enforceability of noncompete agreements (NCAs), we find a significant negative effect on innovation. This effect is even larger for the most novel and innovative patents and firms. Further analysis shows these negative effects on innovation cannot be explained by entry alone and instead likely result from reduced knowledge flows. Our findings suggest that labor mobility plays a crucial role in spreading knowledge across firms. (JEL E24, J08, J21, K31, O31, O33)

title: University as a Melting Pot: Long-Term Effects of Internationalization
abstract: This paper provides the first evidence on the impact of exposure to international students on the long-term outcomes of native students. I combine unique survey and administrative data from the Netherlands covering one million students across three decades and employ an across-cohort design. I find that exposure to international students leads natives to (i) form social ties with nonnatives, (ii) hold more positive attitudes towards migration and learning about other cultures, and (iii) seek opportunities abroad. Notably, I find precisely estimated zero effects on employment, income, entrepreneurship, and the share of international coworkers up to 25 years after university entry. (JEL F22, I23, I26, J15, Z13)

title: Deadwood Labor? The Effects of Eliminating Employment Protection for Older Workers
authors: Emmanuel Saez, Benjamin Schoefer, David Seim
abstract: We analyze mandatory retirement in Sweden, which eliminates employment protection at age 67. Employment falls by about 10 percent and total average earnings by about 20 percent immediately at age 67. Eight percent of jobs separate immediately due to loss of protection, with effects stemming from jobs with stronger initial employment protection (long tenure, firms subject to “last in, first out” rules), and those in the public sector. We examine the effects on continuing jobs. While wages appear rigid, we uncover novel, sizable intensive-margin hours reductions, resulting in an 8 percent drop in earnings conditional on staying on the job. (JEL J14, J22, J26, J31, J63, K31)

title: Environmental stochasticity reduces human planning effort
authors: Jordan Lei, Jeroen Olieslagers, Nastaran Arfaei, Daisy Xinlei Lin, Wei Ji Ma
abstract: The world is stochastic, making planning difficult. Despite the ubiquity of stochasticity in real-world environments, it remains an open question how people effectively balance the cognitive costs of planning against its potential benefits when faced with stochasticity. To study this, we designed a planning task where participants face one of three forms of stochasticity commonly encountered in the real world: reliability, volatility, and controllability. We find a robust pattern across all three manipulations: as stochasticity increases, people reduce their planning effort as measured by first-choice response times. To understand the processes underlying this effect, we developed several computational cognitive models to account for participants’ choices. We find that rather than calculating expected values optimally, people choose a simpler strategy, acting as if the world were deterministic, a phenomenon known as determinizing. Consistent with our response time findings, we find that people reduce their effort by decreasing their sensitivity to values with increasing stochasticity, a signature of policy compression. Our work highlights the often overlooked role of stochasticity in human planning and its impact on planning strategy and effort. Moreover, it reveals the limitations of studying stochasticity solely through single-shot decisions.

title: Religious celibacy is linked to marriage and wealth transmission practices across different world religions
authors: Gabriel Šaffa, Sara Sherbaji, Ruth Mace
abstract: Lifelong religious celibacy may seem to be an evolutionary puzzle. However, it is possible that where siblings compete for parental resources, families can benefit from having some offspring become celibate monks or nuns. Here, we test whether celibacy is more likely to be found in societies with substantial marriage transactions, lower levels of polygyny, and heritable wealth, especially land. Additionally, we predict male celibacy to be linked to polygyny and bride-wealth, and female celibacy to monogamy or polyandry and to dowry. Using Bayesian phylogenetic multilevel models on a cross-cultural sample of 352 societies, we find that celibacy occurs mainly in monogamous societies with heritable wealth, and male and female celibacy are more common where marriage payments are higher for the celibate sex. Buddhism and Christianity are especially likely to institutionalize celibacy, suggesting that the emergence of celibate religious institutions reflects common responses to similar socio-ecological conditions across cultures.

title: Cross-border electricity tariffs undermine power system efficiency, decarbonization and reliability in North America
The effects of participating in government-led citizens’ assemblies
authors: Mariana C. Duarte, Jorge M. Fernandes, Miguel M. Pereira
abstract: Contemporary democracies face growing public disaffection and mistrust. Governments have tried to revert these trends by promoting participatory governance. Prior studies established how deliberation can empower citizens. However, whether these effects hold in real-life initiatives initiated by partisan governments remains unclear. We test the ability of citizens’ assemblies to foster democratic attitudes in a natural experiment leveraging the random selection of participants to Lisbon’s citizens’ assemblies Participation led to an increase in issue knowledge and salience, external political efficacy and institutional trust. However, it did not impact internal political efficacy nor helped citizens better recognize the challenges of collective decision-making. The results hold for two assembly editions and reveal the potential of government-led participatory initiatives to reconnect citizens with democracy.

title: A harmonized European database of education, telework, labour market and earnings from three Eurostat surveys
abstract: VSET is a harmonized cross-survey profile-space resource documenting the alignment of education, occupation, labour-market, telework, establishment size, and earnings variables from three Eurostat surveys. It combines three Eurostat microdata sources accessed under an approved research proposal: the Adult Education Survey (AES) 2022, the Labour Force Survey (LFS) 2023, and the Structure of Earnings Survey (SES) 2018. The final harmonized database contains data for 22 countries, 1,440,134 unique demographic profile cells, 39 variables, and a summed profile multiplicity of 3,249,634. Occupations are standardized using ISCO-08 at the 2-digit level, educational attainment is harmonized into four ISCED-based groupings, and SES earnings are converted to euros before aggregation. The integration workflow uses sequential outer joins and deterministic coalescing of overlapping variables. The final rows describe harmonized profiles rather than linked individuals. The N_instances variable records the multiplicity of identical rows combined during final profile compression. The release has no integrated survey weight. Its rows represent harmonized profile combinations rather than linked respondents or population units, and the dataset is intended for inspecting category mappings, profile coverage, merge compatibility, and reproducible cross-survey processing rather than for population inference.

title: Affective Authority: Understanding Health and Wellness Influence on Social Media
abstract: Health and wellness content has become increasingly popular on social media. When examining why this content resonates with certain viewers, existing research often turns to concepts of authenticity, credibility, trust, expertise, and authority. In this article, we map out existing work on these concepts across an extensive body of interdisciplinary scholarship within media, communication, and cultural studies, and the anthropology of health, media, and medicine. By analyzing how these theories relate to one another, we offer synthesized definitions of them within the context of digital health content. We then make the case that this existing work too often fails to acknowledge the relationality, mediatedness, and affective qualities associated with health and wellness influencers and their content. To combat this, we offer the theoretical intervention of “affective authority,” which encourages an attunement to how affect, emotions, and feelings emerge through the production and consumption of social media content. We argue that this concept of “affective authority” better illuminates how and why wellness influencers and their content are deemed authoritative arbiters of health-related knowledge.

title: Wise Empathy Improves Well-Being on Instagram
authors: Gregory John Depow, Christopher Oveis, Emily Zohar, Michael Inzlicht
abstract: Two-thirds of the global population spends significant time browsing social media, making it critical to understand how to improve online experiences to support well-being. Social media use is often linked to both positive and negative psychological outcomes, but interventions to enhance well-being during social media use remain limited. Here, we test whether an intervention embedded in daily life that trains individuals to use wise empathy on Instagram can improve users’ well-being. Drawing from strategic regulation of empathy and wisdom, we used an ecological momentary intervention to train half our sample ( N = 260) to wisely regulate empathy for positive and negative emotions on their own Instagram feeds. Using experience sampling ( N obs . = 5,902), we tracked empathy and well-being in daily life. The intervention increased wise empathy online – boosting appreciative joy, positive emotion sharing and compassion for negative emotions – while reducing negative emotion sharing, upward social comparisons and personal distress. On surveys where participants had recently browsed Instagram, those in the wise empathy condition reported higher well-being than controls, an effect mediated by changes in wise empathy. These findings position wise empathy as a scalable, trainable skill that can enhance well-being on social media by helping users engage more adaptively with emotional content. This work extends our understanding of how empathy predicts well-being and elucidates the relationship between social media use and well-being, with broad societal implications for our increasingly digital society.

title: Like Walking a Tightrope: User-Centric Perspectives on Content in Need of Moderation
authors: Anna Maria Planitzer, Svenja Schäfer, Pia Pachinger, Sophie Lecheler
abstract: Norm-violating content on social media platforms is on the rise, fueling prejudice and polarization. To counter such developments in a timely manner, platforms rely on automated content moderation. The issue, however, is that current understandings of automated moderation are mostly elite-driven, neglecting individual user perspectives, introducing biases and discrimination, and overlooking that users’ perspectives on what constitutes a norm violation in the first place may differ substantially from those of experts and platforms. Therefore, this study uses focus groups to explore what type of content users themselves think is in need of moderation. Findings suggest that users, while acknowledging the importance of moderating polarized topics (e.g., migration) and uncivil discourse styles (e.g., insults), are more concerned with the motivations of perpetrators and the vulnerability of targets. Our findings show that, if platforms want to incorporate user perspectives when designing automated moderation systems, they must move beyond merely detecting problematic message characteristics and focus on more tailored approaches, alongside accountability measures for perpetrators and safety measures for victims.

title: Scrolling for the Truth: Source Factors, Persuasion, and a Test of Misinformation Interventions on TikTok
authors: Brittany N. Shivers Weinstein, Bartosz W. Wojdynski
abstract: The popularity of the video-based social media platform TikTok has rapidly grown in recent years, and with it its role in rapidly disseminating misinformation to its relatively young user base. However, little is known to date about how users perceive misinformation or about how platform interventions could be deployed to stop its spread. Two experiments examined users’ perceptions of TikTok videos making claims about a current health issue (monkeypox). Study 1 tested the impact of information type (true vs. false) and source (journalist vs. influencer) on users’ perceptions of TikTok videos, with party identification as a moderator. Participants rated message credibility and source quality higher for true videos and videos with a journalistic source. Study 2 tested the efficacy of three potential misinformation interventions (a banner label, pre-roll video, and click-through warning) and the role of psychological reactance. There was a main effect of the banner label and public service announcement pre-roll video on perceived message credibility. The interventions had no main effect on source quality, but there was a mediation of the PSA pre-roll and banner label on credibility and quality perceptions through reactance. In both studies, participants had difficulty discerning between true and false claims. Implications for journalists and social media companies are discussed, along with suggestions for future research.

title: Migration and Cities in Chile: Building Territories of Solidarity in Hostile Contexts
authors: María Fernanda Stang, Carolina Stefoni, Aline Bravo, Víctor Félix Da Silva
abstract: This article analyzes practices identified at the territorial level in Antofagasta, a city in northern Chile. These practices have successfully established infrastructures of solidarity between the national and migrant populations, resulting in what we refer to as territories of solidarity. Following Schillinger’s work (2020), we argue that within these territories, experiences of solidarity emerge through contentious processes stemming from daily coexistence in a group of informal settlements (known as campamentos in Chile), mutual support efforts, the creation of alliances, and the production of (counter)spaces and (counter)knowledge. These practices of solidarity take on configurations linked to the organized social fabric in this territory and to the relationships forged with governmental, institutional, and organized actors at different levels. This experience not only emerges and coexists but also suffers and resists hostile migration policies, along with a hegemonic discourse that criminalizes and otherizes migrants.
journal_full: Journal of Race, Ethnicity and Politics

title: The Supply of Demands: What Black Lives Matter Demanded in 2020
abstract: Despite the significant role social media played in mobilizing Black Lives Matter supporters, political science research on this topic focuses on the years before the massive mobilizations in 2020. This paper draws on a novel dataset of BLM chapters’ tweets during the George Floyd protests to examine the language activists used to facilitate protests during the movement’s peak public support. Despite having more experience mobilizing followers, older chapters were less likely to encourage followers to pursue change through conventional electoral politics even in the midst of a presidential election year. Instead, older chapters were more likely to share educational resources or media that cultivated a collective identity among supporters and followers.

title: Selfish and prosocial individuals both distort their actions’ impact, but selfish distortions can be more contagious
abstract: People often act without knowing exactly how their actions impact others. Here, across nine preregistered online experiments ( N = 8,769 adults, predominantly US residents), we tested whether people exploit this ambiguity to make themselves look good. On average, selfish individuals inflated the social benefit of their choice while downplaying that of the alternative, reporting the two options as more similar than prosocial individuals did (experiment 1a: b = 0.24, 95% confidence interval 0.14–0.34). Prosocial individuals portrayed their choice as comparatively more socially beneficial; they also inflated their implied relative sacrifice, although less consistently. We observed distortions even before people made a choice and when choices were forced, consistent with distortions reflecting social preferences rather than mere justification. While people differed in whether and how they distorted, distortions favouring selfishness showed evidence of contagion: others adopted them and became more selfish (experiment 6, selfish-serving versus no-distortion: b = 0.49, 95% confidence interval 0.10–0.88). These findings offer a psychological foundation for why polarized positions about the social impact of one’s actions may emerge. When social consequences are open to interpretation, people may predictably form divergent interpretations.

title: From collective action to collective rescue: rethinking distribution and cooperation in climate governance under common peril

When Digital Exposure Meets Everyday Buying: Understanding Consumer Behaviour in FMCG
abstract: Consumers today may discover a product on social media, encounter it repeatedly through digital advertising, and still make the final purchase from a neighbourhood store. This study explores the relationship between digital exposure and everyday consumer behaviour in the fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) sector. Using a consumer survey dataset containing 26 usable responses, the study examines purchase frequency, purchase channels, exposure to social-media promotions, reported influence of online advertising, customer satisfaction, and recommendation intention. The findings show that social-media exposure is relatively common, while reported influence of online advertising is more mixed. Traditional retail remains important, with kirana stores and supermarkets accounting for most reported purchase channels. Mean satisfaction was 3.92 out of 5 among respondents with valid satisfaction scores, while recommendation intention was predominantly positive. Exploratory statistical analysis did not identify a statistically significant association between online-ad influence and recommendation intention (χ² = 0.26, p = 0.61), nor a statistically significant relationship between satisfaction and recommendation intention (Spearman ρ ≈ 0.21, p ≈ 0.31). The findings suggest that digital visibility should not automatically be interpreted as behavioural influence. Consumer decisions appear to involve a broader combination of digital communication, product experience, purchasing convenience, availability, and customer service. Given the small and youth-concentrated sample, the study is exploratory and does not claim population-level generalizability. The paper highlights the need for larger and more diverse studies examining how digital engagement interacts with the wider FMCG consumer journey.

title: Human Circuits in Cold War Taiwan: RCA, Labour Governance, and the Developmental State
abstract: Industrial development depends on institutions that organise technological learning and govern production. In Cold War Taiwan, these institutions also shaped who could challenge industrial harm. Drawing on field research, interviews, legal records, and institutional histories, this article argues that Taiwan’s developmental capacity was selective. A paired history of RCA Taiwan and the separate RCA-ITRI technology transfer project shows how investment promotion and labour governance privileged officially selected industrial objectives over workers’ independent authority. Public sponsorship equipped semiconductor learning with personnel, facilities, and foreign knowledge. Labour administration, managed representation, and corporate control of hazard information restricted workers’ demands for protection. Pay, housing, and production routines made exposure difficult to avoid, while repeated inspections failed to secure compliance. Missing records, withheld information, and corporate restructuring then obstructed compensation claims. Workers and their supporters challenged these barriers by assembling legal, scientific, and archival resources. Their struggle places labour protection within the history of developmental capacity, alongside the acquisition of technology.

title: Explaining historical persistence in Germany's electoral geography across 130 years: a cleavage-perspective on continuity in spatial patterns of party support
abstract: This article studies the long-run persistence of electoral geographies. Drawing on cleavage theory, I argue that spatial patterns of party support persist where cleavages remain politically salient and the social groups they mobilise stay in place. I evidence this argument for Germany, combining electoral and census data from the German Empire (1890–1912) and reunified Germany (2002–2021) at the municipality, county and electoral-district level. The spatial analyses reveal substantial continuity in the electoral geographies of the mainstream left and right. The analysis traces both to one source, the persistent spatial distribution of Catholics. Christian democrats continued historical strongholds of the Center Party where Catholics stayed concentrated, while the SPD persists as its mirror image in the non-Catholic space. Persistence therefore rests on the stability of the religious geography and cleavage, not on the class cleavage and the economic geography, which has changed markedly. The findings position cleavage-based persistence as a complement to cultural-transmission accounts of historical legacies, locating continuity in the ongoing mobilisation of stable social groups rather than in transmitted attitudes alone.

title: Why Politicians Retweet: News Trustworthiness, Emotion, and Partisan Asymmetry in Elite News Sharing among US Congress Members
authors: Apeksha Shetty, Esther Simmendinger, Jula Lühring, Annie Waldherr, David Garcia, Hannah Metzler
abstract: On social media, politicians' retweets can determine which claims gain visibility in online and in wider political debate, yet the factors associated with these retweeting decisions remain poorly understood. Combining natural language processing measures of emotional tone and partisan cues with politician-level characteristics, we analyze the retweeting behavior of United States Members of Congress between 2021 and 2023 using multilevel logistic regression models. Using all news-related retweets during this period, paired with a negative sample of non-retweets, we examine how tweet content and legislators' ideological extremity predict the amplification of tweets linking to more and less trustworthy news domains. We find that partisan identity is a stronger predictor of retweeting than other factors. While politicians generally preferred retweeting content with links to trustworthy sources, this preference weakened when tweets contained party-related references. Anger and fear predicted higher retweeting likelihood when tweets referenced political opponents, while anger predicted lower retweeting likelihood when tweets referenced political allies. Furthermore, ideology conditioned how politicians responded to news trustworthiness: among Republicans, increasing ideological extremity was associated with weaker preference for trustworthy sources, with the most ideologically-extreme Republicans being especially likely to retweet tweets with links to less trustworthy domains. Together, these results suggest that politicians use retweets to reinforce partisan boundaries between 'us' and 'them'. This identity-centered pattern to retweeting explains how information from less trustworthy sources gains traction in polarized digital environments.

title: When the Children’s Rights Normative Culture (CRNC) is Full of Holes: The Child’s Right to Mental Health in Post-Conflict Sool and Sanaag
authors: Guleid Ahmed Jama, Marieke J. Hopman
abstract: This paper aims to understand the situation of children’s mental health rights in Sool and Sanaag. We apply the Children’s Rights Normative Culture (CRNC) model (Hopman et al. 2026) to a dataset of 85 research conversation conducted between May and November 2025 (40 children, 45 adults) in the two cities. A key finding from the research is that children’s mental health is not recognised as a distinct rights issue within the socio-legal orders applicable in the research area. Moreover, there is no clearly articulated or enforceable socio-legal obligation (from any socio-legal order) concerning the protection of children’s mental health. Nor do the socio-legal norms seem to establish specific remedial measures for children experiencing mental health difficulties. The language of rights is largely absent from people’s understanding of children’s mental health. Across clan, community, religious, and state normative orders, children are mainly seen through the family framework. The paper suggest that 1) children’s mental health should be seen as a children’s rights, 2) families, particularly mothers, and the community, should be engaged as key entry point for societal change, 3) space should be created for children where they can safely share their experiences and views at all levels, including the family, schools, community and post-conflict peacebuilding initiatives.

title: Agreement Without Accuracy: Six Systematic Defects an LLM Annotation Study Could Not See in Its Own Reliability Statistics
abstract: Researchers who use large language models as annotators are commonly asked to demonstrate reliability, and test–retest agreement under a fixed seed is the cheapest evidence. We report a study in which it was systematically misleading. Annotating 1,902 student UML class specifications under a fixed snapshot, seed and zero temperature, we compared three prompt configurations, each run twice. A three-stage pipeline appeared to raise answer-level agreement from .647 to .845, with chance-corrected agreement rising for every code and internal consistency satisfied throughout. Comparing per-code prevalence led us to inspect outputs; five systematic defects emerged: an instruction promising an input never supplied (wrong on 64.7% of its flags at κ = .971); a stage receiving element names stripped of the types it was to judge; residual error after repair; enumerated conditions firing outside their scope; and alignment tables stored without half of what they summarised. A sixth lay in our checking procedure: the audit rule we wrote agreed with a blind reading on only 67.5% of cases, and the twenty cases read to confirm it were drawn from its own output. A blind reading of forty random submissions, judged before any output was seen, is the study's only anchored estimate; under it our one reported repair cannot be shown to help. None was surfaced by a reliability statistic; those that altered the model's inputs or rules raised agreement by easing its task. Reliability from repeated runs should be accompanied by prevalence comparisons and a sample read blind, drawn independently of the detector.

title: Cultural Cognitive Scaffolding
abstract: In many domains, human life has undergone dramatic changes—globalized exchanges, complex technological systems, large societies—that would both require and result from rapid cognitive change. In this work, I introduce the Cultural Cognitive Scaffolding Hypothesis, which posits that (1) human cognition is uniquely culturally evolvable because our cognitive processes rely on environmental resources that are largely culturally evolvable, and, as a consequence, (2) it is these specific cultural innovations, called cultural cognitive scaffolds (CCS), that are responsible for much of the rapid, recent changes in human cognition. Importantly, to achieve this effect, these cultural innovations must balance cognitive impact and cultural success. The historical expansion of exchange networks offers an ideal case to illustrate how diverse cultural innovations helped manage the high uncertainty associated with exchanges across larger physical and cultural distances, and a window into how cultural success can be achieved for different cultural innovations. Finally, this framework has important implications for our understanding of the uniquely open-ended character of human culture.

title: Identifying determinants of ecological footprints: A novel application of latent growth curve models (LGM)
abstract: This study investigates the determinants of ecological footprint growth trajectories in 112 countries (2004–2017) using latent growth curve models (LGM). Unlike traditional panel methods, LGM captures dynamic trends and country-level heterogeneity in environmental impact over time. The approach integrates economic, institutional, and socio-geographic determinants into a unified causal framework. Results indicate that economic complexity mediates the relationship between economic growth and ecological footprint, promoting technological innovation and sustainable practices. Higher economic complexity also partially offsets environmental impacts from increased fossil fuel consumption. These findings underscore the need for policies fostering innovation, economic diversification, and sustainable urban planning to mitigate environmental degradation.

title: Determinants of the relationship between growth and CO2 emissions: A novel application utilizing bivariate latent growth curve models (BLGM) across European regions
abstract: This study investigates the key determinants shaping the dynamic relationship between economic growth and CO2 emissions in 220 European NUTS2 regions from 2000 to 2021, using a bivariate latent growth curve model (BLGM). Unlike traditional methods, the BLGM framework addresses a critical gap in modeling latent growth processes, variable interactions, and regional heterogeneity, significantly advancing previous methodologies. The approach integrates determinants of regional economic structures, energy consumption patterns, labor market characteristics, and educational attainment. The results highlight the crucial role of financial structure, spatial centrality, and educated development, offering insights for adaptive and effective regional climate and sustainability strategies and emphasizing the need for coordinated policies that integrate technological innovation, territorial planning, labor market diversification, and sustained investment in education.

title: Examination of the News-Finds-Me Perception as an Expanded Bifactor Construct
abstract: Within the mass and political communication literatures, the news-find-me (NFM) perception has been increasingly used to explain the democratically deleterious implications of a reliance on incidental, socially mediated news contact. Despite these efforts, there does not currently exist a consistent means of measuring the NFM construct. This study developed an expanded NFM measure and evaluated it using a latent bifactor model specification. The results suggested that a bifactor-(S·I 1) specification fit the data in a plausible manner, and, therein, that there exist research scenarios where the use of such an approach may confer benefits to researchers.

title: From Affective Experience to Mechanism: A Critical Realist Case Study Architecture Using Reflexive Thematic Analysis
abstract: Studying affective life qualitatively poses a known problem. Burnout, emotional labour, and slow shifts in teacher–class relations are real with measurable effects, yet not directly visible; we infer them from behaviour and language. Interpretation always mediates. How can we claim mechanisms without pretending to observe them? This paper proposes a case-study architecture using reflexive thematic analysis within a critical realist frame. It integrates five usually separate elements: a multi-perspectival case design; abduction and retroduction as genuinely different inferences; systematic assessment of rival explanations; a procedure for sorting context from mechanism when they do not separate cleanly; and a hierarchy of claims calibrated to evidence. The combination yields what neither purely interpretive nor purely causal work can: fallible mechanism explanations that take meaning and causation equally seriously. The argument is specified, not demonstrated. Two computational simulations provide proof of concept. The first distinguishes two known ground-truth mechanisms across 40 synthetic cases, with 80% overall recovery (95% CI [68%, 92%]; 85% and 75% per mechanism). The second adds a third rival—perceptual reconstruction, in which teacher behaviour is unchanged but students report change—and distinguishes all three across 60 synthetic cases, with 95% overall recovery (100%, 100%, 85%). The three-way test uses tighter noise parameters than the two-way, so rates are not directly comparable. Both test only one component and neither substitutes for empirical validation on real classroom data, which remains future work.

title: Ideology on the U.S. District Courts: Reexamining Presidential and Senatorial Appointment Power
authors: Nicholas O. Howard, David A Hughes, Philip Warncke
abstract: Unlike U.S. appellate courts, scholars of the American federal judiciary typically lack ideological estimates for district court judges that are derived directly from their behavior. Rather, scholars have primarily relied upon proxy measures based upon the preferences of a judge's appointing president or those of home-state senators in the event senatorial courtesy is in effect. Nevertheless, senatorial courtesy is a norm, and norms can be broken. It remains an open question whether home-state senators genuinely constrain the president when it comes to the ideological tenor of appointees to the district courts. We produce novel ideal point estimates for 1,680 U.S.~district court judges appointed between 1913 and 2009 based upon their votes in approximately 100,000 cases, in addition to contextual factors unique to judges and the process by which they were appointed. We map these ideal points into the Judicial Common Space and make them publicly available to American courts scholars. These ideal points differ meaningfully compared to previous proxy measures and improve predictive power in judge voting behavior. Importantly, despite a battery of statistical tests, we find that senatorial courtesy appears to play a minimal role with respect to the revealed preferences of U.S. district court judges compared to the role the president's ideology plays. If senatorial courtesy indeed constrains presidents in the separation of powers game, it is likely on some other, non-ideological dimension.

title: Staying Connected: Methodological Insights for Developing Panel Surveys with People Experiencing Homelessness
authors: Caroline Teague, Aryaa Rajouria, Yuanxi Li, Brandon Morande, Hugo Aguas, Nathalie Williams, Jerald Herting, ihsan kahveci
abstract: Longitudinal research on people experiencing homelessness remains rare due to challenges in sustained contact, digital access, and institutional trust. This study draws on three focus groups conducted between September 2024 and January 2025 in King County, Washington, to explore how to tailor contact modes in longitudinal surveys with persons experiencing homelessness to improve retention and reduce attrition. Participants highlighted major barriers to digital contact, including inconsistent access to phones and service, charging stations, and two-factor authentication. Email was preferred for its stability. Participants emphasized the need for transparent, scheduled communication and flexible incentives, such as Cash app. We conclude with a summary of practical suggestions to improve survey design and discuss how our findings from one particular setting can be extended more broadly around the country and world.

title: The Substitution Trap: Development Aid and the Composition of Government Spending in Indian States
abstract: The question of whether aid supplements or substitutes government spending has long been debated in public finance literature. Building on Vadlamannati and Iacono (2026), who examine how development aid affects discretionary fiscal transfers to Indian states, we address a distinct fiscal question: how does aid exposure affect the composition of subnational government expenditure? Using panel data for 30 Indian states over 1979-2019 (41 years) and an instrumental variable strategy addressing potential endogeneity, we find that greater exposure to aid is associated with a lower share of capital expenditure and a higher share of revenue expenditure. This pattern is consistent with substitution of externally aided projects for domestically financed spending. The effect however varies systematically with electoral incentives. In states with greater electoral competition, aid is more strongly associated with capital expenditure, suggesting that electoral incentives can encourage state governments to channel external resources towards visible capital investments. Our findings extend the evidence on fiscal consequences of aid in India from the allocation of intergovernmental discretionary transfers to the composition of state government expenditure. Our findings reveal that the developmental effects of aid depend not only on how resources reach subnational governments but also on how governments subsequently allocate them.

title: Data visualization: Spanish results in PISA across waves by parental educational attainment
abstract: Using Spanish PISA microdata from 2003–2025, we analyze performance trends in mathematics and reading by parental educational attainment. Results show a steady decline in scores among students from highly educated families, starting as early as 2012 in mathematics and 2015 in reading.

title: Disaffording the Pedestrian: When Affordances Are Removed
abstract: Designing for pedestrian road safety is challenging. Designs need to work for a broad and diverse range of pedestrians, while also considering the needs of other vulnerable road users, such as cyclists. Pedestrians are ranked as the most vulnerable in the road user hierarchy and designing for those with protected characteristics is critically important for road safety designers. One key challenge faced is designing the environment so that safety provisions can align with national and international goals to encourage people to walk or wheel more for health, economic and environmental reasons. Doctoral research was undertaken to understand whether and how design can improve pedestrian road safety and used key study sites in London to investigate the relationship between safety affordances in public space and pedestrian safety. One main finding was that often, during a redesign, safety features are removed. The consequences of these changes make it difficult for pedestrians to maintain their safety, particularly those with protected characteristics. Beyond potential physical harm, there are psychosocial impacts: people may avoid a route if they feel it is unsafe or leads to conflict in contested spaces which leaves pedestrians feeling unable to navigate a space confidently. These experiences are not routinely captured within road safety data, which focuses largely on KSI (killed or seriously injured) outcomes. I have coined this phenomenon of removing an affordance a disaffordance. The concept comes from over five years of doctoral research into pedestrian road safety in the UK, which focused on pedestrian-only study sites in London that had been redesigned as shared-space zones. Identifying safety affordances and disaffordances in the built environment helps to identify opportunities for broader and more systematic pedestrian participation in the design process. The research also developed GroundMap, a diagnostic approach for identifying and mapping affordances and disaffordances and anticipating the potential consequences of their removal. At a broader level, the term disaffordance might be extended to identify other environments where the removal of an affordance has significant consequences. While this research applies the concept specifically to pedestrian safety, its wider application across other environments and domains is identified here as a direction for future work.

title: Monetary Policy Transmission in Nepal: A Study of How Central Bank Policy Rates Affect Bank Lending and Economic Activity
abstract: Monetary policy transmission, the mechanism through which the monetary policy of the central bank impacts bank lending rates and, by extension, the broader economy, is of great interest to policymakers. This paper provides an in-depth analysis of the monetary policy transmission mechanism in the Nepalese context. It focuses on the interest rate pass-through channels and associated frictions in the Nepalese monetary policy framework. It uses the information published by NRB, the central bank of Nepal, as well as scholarly research and reports on the topic to perform the study. It highlights that the interest rate pass-through in Nepal is partial and delayed and discusses the reason why monetary policy transmissions in Nepal work as they do. The paper starts with an introduction to the topic of monetary policy transmission. Then, it proceeds to discuss research questions and objectives, theoretical background, and methodological background. Finally, it presents data analysis and discusses the findings to reach final conclusions and recommendations.

title: External Debt Sustainability in Nepal: A Case Study Based on Nepal Rastra Bank, IMF, and World Bank Data
abstract: External debt sustainability is a matter of great concern for many developing countries like Nepal since a part of the borrowed money is regarded as the liability that threatens to criticize the value of their local currency and increases their fiscal burden. This paper performs an analysis of the external debt indicators of Nepal and the risk of a debt distress using the information provided by Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank. According to the results, the total public debt in Nepal is expected to reach about Rs 2.97 trillion (USD 19.21 billion) by the end of fiscal year 2025/26, which is equivalent to 45.07 percent of GDP, as compared to 43.79 percent in the previous year. The external debt increased to about 25.3 percent of GDP from 20.6 percent, and that of domestic one remained at about 22-23 percent. Nepal still belongs to the countries with low risk of experiencing a debt distress, according to the joint World Bank-IMF Debt Sustainability Analysis (DSA). However, the study highlights several vulnerabilities in the external debt of Nepal as the present value of the external debt-to-exports ratio exceeds the indicative threshold in the export shock scenario. The Nepali rupee has depreciated by around Rs 8 against the US dollar in the first seven months of FY2025/26, adding Rs 92.96 billion to the external debt of the country. Only around one-third of the capital budget has been spent, which implies that the borrowed money is used for sustaining the recurrent expenditure rather than capital spending. The paper concludes that Nepal’s debt is sustainable in the near term. However, the increasing vulnerabilities in the form of currency depreciation, inadequate revenue mobilization efforts and low efficiency utilization of the borrowed funds should be responded to in order to address long-term sustainability.

title: Turning Ambition into Action: Lessons from the Italian National Recovery and Resilience Plan
authors: Alessia Aspide, Lorenzo Mascioli, Gabriele Beretta, Camilla Locatelli
abstract: The Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) is the primary financial instrument of the EU’s ambitious pandemic response initiative, NextGenerationEU (NGEU). This report examines Italy’s capacity to implement its ambitious National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NRRP) effectively. It opens with a comparative analysis of the NRRPs of the four largest EU economies: Germany, France, Italy, and Spain. Focusing then on Italy, the largest recipient, the report explores how state capacity shapes the implementation of ambitious reforms and investments, emphasizing the challenges of translating NGEU’s transformative goals into tangible outcomes.

title: Issues and Challenges of Poverty and International Labor Migration in Nepal
abstract: This paper aims to discuss the opportunity and challenges of the foreign labor market for Nepalese workers and Nepal’s government policy. The study was carried out in the form of a qualitative research method, where secondary data were used. The collected data were analyzed using the content analysis method after a close reading of the sources. This paper discussed the current situation of government policy, manpower agencies, problems of migrant workers, and the way of using the remittance. This research found that the government policy is less effective, and manpower agencies are not following the government rules and regulations. Since the last two decades, remittances have been a significant contributor to the Nepalese economy. Many scholars argued that remittance helps to reduce the country’s poverty rates. However, Nepalese workers face numerous problems in the home country and destination countries. Migrant workers are being charged high service charges and misguided by the local agent and manpower agencies in the home country Nepal. They face problems in destination countries such as low remuneration, sexual abuse, and risky job environment. Most of the remittances are using daily expenses such as purchasing foods. This paper explores these vulnerabilities of migrant workers and suggests stakeholder interventions to make safer migration and sustainably use a remittance.

title: Women's Land Rights in India: A Learning Document
authors: ISST, Jahnvi Andharia, Benu Verma, Saee Pawar, Ashmeet Kaur, Kritika Goel
abstract: Womanity has decided to strategically accelerate gender equality and economic empowerment of women in India by developing and supporting sustainable models that look at women's land rights pathways that can be adapted and scaled across the country. The program focuses on increasing land literacy, women’s land ownership and long-term land access to secure livelihoods for 50,000 women at the community level. Womanity’s Theory of Change (ToC) Document outlines the rationale and the pathway to advance gender equality and economic empowerment of women through sustainable models and strategic interventions. Womanity has outlined three phases to reach 50,000 women – Build, Enhance and Scale. In the Build phase, it seeks to identify challenges, evolve prototype sustainable models, measure effectiveness and impact, support implements, invest in research, and develop a comprehensive evidence plan. This learning document prepared by ISST contributes to the efforts of the Build phase of Womanity. The objective of this document is to capture the learnings of the various partner organizations, key members of the Womanity team, and the other stakeholders (referred as the Womanity ecosystem in India) in the first 18 months of the project period, as well as their future learning needs. Through a thorough analysis of the data collected over six months, a learning framework was expected to map all possible needs for building knowledge and strengthening capacities within the Womanity ecosystem to effectively address various WLR issues

title: Long-Term Sequences of State-Building and Violent Conflict
abstract: A large body of research demonstrates that state capacity is an important correlate of intrastate conflict. However, similar levels of present-day state capacity can result from different historical trajectories of state-building. I argue that specific sequences of state-building can shape the risk of violent conflict in the long run: geographical obstacles can isolate territories from state-building processes for extended periods, strengthening non-state institutions. The risk of violence increases once the state has accumulated sufficient capabilities to close this state-building gap. The extension of authority into peripheral territories triggers resistance from among local elites that mobilize their constituencies against the central state. I exploit exogenous variation in early state-penetration in Nepal to investigate this argument. Areas located below the Himalayan foothills were heavily Malaria-infested preventing the state from establishing meaningful presence until the implementation of a malaria eradication program in the 1950/60s. I make use of this specificity in Regression Discontinuity (RD) estimations. The findings lend support to the primary arguments of the paper and underscore the role of long-term sequences of development.

title: Rounding and the bill-size gradient in tipping
abstract: Restaurant tip percentages often decline as bills increase. Rounding is one proposed explanation because a fixed upward adjustment adds more to the tip percentage on a small bill. We examine how much of the observed decline can be explained by adjustments of up to one dollar. We analyzed 22,446 checks with positive recorded tips, no automatic gratuity and bills of $10–$200 from three North Carolina restaurant outlets. For checks with a whole-dollar tip or reconstructed final payment, we allowed the pre-rounding tip to fall anywhere from one dollar below the recorded amount to the recorded amount, with a minimum of zero. We calculated the smallest and largest bill-size coefficients across these possible amounts, controlling for outlet, month, guest count, opening hour and weekday. Bootstrap checks resampled dates, weeks and servers. Each scheme used 999 draws, with the rounding bounds recalculated for each resampled dataset. Tip percentages fell by 4.29 points per bill doubling. Even the adjustments that most reduce this decline leave a coefficient of −1.62 points, which remains negative across all three bootstrap checks. Five-dollar rounding or restricting bills to $30–$200 allows the fitted decline to disappear. Upward dollar rounding cannot fully explain the negative gradient in the primary sample. Larger rounding increments and the exclusion of small bills produce ranges containing zero.

title: Antagonistic Predictions
abstract: Why do we use models to predict the most likely outcome? Integrating model predictions into high-stakes decision-making pipelines can amplify biases and introduce flawed decisions when human caseworkers and models compete over the same prediction target. Learning to anticipate the most likely outcome risks reproducing biases embedded in historical data, while delivering such predictions in human-AI decision-making raises issues of cognitive biases and algorithmic aversion versus overreliance. In this perspective, I argue for Antagonistic Predictions, a structurally different paradigm where models are tasked to act as sparring partners that challenge human pre-conceptions and show reachable futures rather than anticipating the most common pattern. I envision instantiations of Antagonistic Predictions that can counteract historical disadvantages, social stereotyping, and cognitive biases and sketch potential implementations in predictive ML and generative AI settings.

title: A Geographic Accessibility Database for Health Care Services to Support Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias Exposome Research
authors: Amber DeJohn, Kyusik Kim, Weining Kan
abstract: These datasets characterize geographic access to health care providers that are associated with modifiable risk factors for Alzheimer’s Disease and Alzheimer’s Disease-related Dementias (AD/ADRD) for the United States. We offer three measures of geographic access, including the drive time to the closest provider (i.e., nearest facility), how many providers are within a 30, 60, 90, and 120-minute drive (i.e., cumulative opportunity), and the Minimum Attainment Cost (MAC), a new measure that facilitates urban-rural comparisons at a national scale. As an intermediary data product, we provide the origin-destination matrices that are used to generate geographic access measures. We calculate geographic access scores for thirteen types of healthcare facilities at the census block group scale and provide population-weighted aggregate measures at the census tract. Researchers can use these data in tandem with demographic information and other place-based measures to characterize the reachable health care landscape in order to understand how access to care may influence modifiable risk factors for AD/ADRD.

title: Sustaining Imbalance: International Financial Foundations of Growth Models
authors: Benjamin Braun, Lucio Baccaro, Joshua Cova
abstract: Current account imbalances, which have surged again in recent years, are key drivers of global economic instability and conflict. Political economy explanations tend to focus on wage restraint and currency undervaluation. However, in a world of unrestricted cross-border capital mobility, the binding constraint for sustaining imbalances over time is financial flows. To address this gap, we develop a theoretical framework linking current account imbalances, growth models, and domestic financialization. We hypothesize that deep and liquid financial markets enable the reproduction of consumption-led growth by relaxing the current account constraint, while financial underdevelopment favors export-led growth by incentivizing capital exports. We test our theoretical propositions with a series of error correction models and an event history analysis, based on panel data on 55 countries over the period 1970-2022. We find broad support for the theoretical expectations but a dissimilarity in the relationship between growth models and financialization: While financial development is crucial for the long-term maintenance of consumption-led growth in advanced economies especially, results are inconclusive regarding the role of financial underdevelopment as a facilitating factor for export-led growth.

title: JCGE: A Modular Julia Framework for Computable General Equilibrium Modelling
abstract: Computable general equilibrium (CGE) modelling requires a workflow beyond equilibrium specification and solution: data preparation, calibration, model construction, diagnostics, experiments, and results handling. JCGE is an Apache-2.0-licensed Julia framework of focused, independently versioned packages. It provides data and calibration utilities, reusable CGE blocks, a shared execution specification, diagnostics, outputs, and reference models. Application packages compose these components while retaining their own data, closures, and economic assumptions. The runtime constructs JuMP models for nonlinear and mixed-complementarity formulations without prescribing a solver. A Model Context Protocol interface supports framework discovery and owner-registered workflows. This paper presents the architecture, quality controls, and reuse potential for independently developed CGE software.

title: Calling Capitalism and Class in the United States: From Reconstruction and the Gilded Age to the Present
abstract: This article explains how American capitalism repeatedly transformed rather than displaced the moral language of calling. Beginning with Reconstruction and the Gilded Age, it traces how disciplined labor, self-command, thrift, and achievement were detached from Calvinist theology and reembedded in corporations, schools, professions, credit systems, welfare institutions, and digitally mediated workplaces. It develops an institutional account of moralized inequality: institutions distribute unequal resources and opportunities, then classify unequal outcomes as individual merit, responsibility, or failure. The analysis distinguishes property, organizational authority, expertise, income, wealth, employment security, debt exposure, and institutional dependence, while showing how race, gender, citizenship, education, occupation, and locality convert historically unequal resources into apparently individual merit. Calling persists as a contested moral infrastructure of capitalism. The central question is whether institutions that demand effort, commitment, and self-investment can justify the unequal security, authority, wealth, and recognition that follow.

title: Dignity Defense Model : A Study on the Structural Mismatch in Employment of Female University Students in China and Its Shaping Mechanism on the Decline in Fertility Rate
abstract: Millions of female university graduates in China face a severe shortage of standardized office jobs with weekends off each year. This structural mismatch exacerbates employment pressure. Drawing on empirical data from the Anhui provincial civil service examination, this paper proposes a “dignity-defense-oriented reproductive decision-making model.” Confronted with the gap between high career expectations and labor-market reality, female university students, motivated by dignity defense and risk aversion toward the motherhood penalty, prefer survival strategies such as “slow employment” and the “civil service examination craze” over marriage and childbearing. These choices significantly suppress the overall birth rate. To address this dilemma, the paper recommends reconstructing the university employment-quality evaluation system and disciplinary structure, introducing national policies that reduce the motherhood penalty, and promoting a shift in the macro-market toward consumption infrastructure centered on independent women.

title: An Assessment of the Vanderbilt-Washington University Report on Sociology
abstract: The Sociology portion of the Vanderbilt-Washington University Report (VWUR) claims to have studied the discipline of sociology and asserts that sociology’s search for truth has been compromised by what the author calls “politicization.” I find that the VWUR’s claims are unsubstantiated and based upon fundamental errors. The problem is not lack of data but rather that the author, Dr. Ashley Rubin, misunderstands and misrepresents the data she does have while failing to check her own biases. She mistakenly reads politicization into everything she sees, reaffirming a thesis she had already held before her supposedly impartial study without taking the appropriate steps to suspend her bias. The VWUR violates the very social scientific standards that it purports to defend while distracting us from other problems facing social science.

title: What the World Studies, Invents and Reports About Urban Heat
abstract: We assemble 20,422 scholarly papers on urban heat islands (1990–2025), read the 17,101 that carry an abstract sentence by sentence, and join them to 96,726 news articles (2021–2025), 4,123 patent families, 14,576 recorded heat incidents, registers of companies, funding rounds and government funding events, and the annual accounts of Indian companies. Eight results stand out. (1) The field grew about 9 times faster than the scholarly literature as a whole, and in 2015–2019 titles naming "extreme heat" overtook those naming "heat island". (2) Of 2,409 papers that attribute urban heat to a cause, 48% name urbanisation and land-use change; attribution to anthropogenic heat fell from 18.4% to 7.7%. (3) Research and news describe different problems: at equal text length, 28% of research openings raise mitigation against 1.6% of news leads, while 22% of news leads are forecasts or warnings against 1.4% of research. (4) They also describe different places: China accounts for 31% of the research and 2.3% of English-language coverage, and Delhi receives 7.4 times the coverage its research share would predict. (5) Invention has outrun science: patent families for cool and permeable pavements grew 12-fold in a decade against 2.4-fold for the research on them. (6) Across 194 studies the median reported cooling from urban trees is 2.0 °C (air temperature 2.0 °C, surface temperature 2.9 °C). (7) Between 2021–22 and 2024–25 news coverage moved from the hazard to the people exposed: workers, schools, the elderly and hospital patients each rose 1.4- to 2.4-fold as a share of heat articles while wildfire and drought fell by about half and climate change — raised in about one article in ten — fell by a quarter. (8) The market record is thin: 140 of 5.05 million companies state a heat or cooling purpose, and recorded capital is $2.7 billion of cooling-infrastructure finance against $48 million of venture funding; larger Indian cooling companies grew revenue 25% a year over three years against 16% for Indian companies generally. Every cause category extracted from the research was tested against an independent second reader; three failed, and no result reported here rests on them.

title: Financial Sector Stability and Credit Growth in Nepal: A Case Study
abstract: Nepal’s financial system has undergone waves of credit booms, especially in the pre- and post-COVID-19 pandemic periods, which raises questions about the health of the banking sector. This paper examines the association between credit growth and banking sector health using secondary data from Nepal Rastra Bank and the International Monetary Fund. The World Bank for fiscal years 2016/17-2023/24. It is found that private sector credit grew at nearly 29 percent in 2016/17 and more than 27 percent in 2020/21, which far exceeded the overall economy’s growth rates. Credit boomed due to large remittance inflows, low real interest rates, and rapid expansion of bank outlets and digital products. Heavy lending to real estate, housing, construction, and import sectors. Consequently, the quality of banks’ assets declined as credit growth slowed down sharply in 2021/22. The non-performing loan ratio, which averaged between 1.2 and 1.8 percent during the boom years, rose to about 2.6 percent in 2022/23 and 3.7 percent in 2023/24. The capital adequacy ratio of banks dipped from 14.5 percent in 2016/17 to 12.8 percent in 2023/24. The study concludes that rapid credit growth, albeit beneficial for a short time, may pose significant financial stability risks if the lending environment worsens and credit becomes concentrated in a few sectors. The paper recommends enhanced risk-based supervision, countercyclical capital buffers, diversification of credit to productive sectors, improved governance, and enhanced capital markets to complement bank lending

title: Social Ecology and Diagnostic Visibility: A Cross-National Analysis of Autism Spectrum Disorder Prevalence in 55 Countries
abstract: Cross-national variation in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) prevalence is commonly attributed to differences in diagnostic infrastructure and case ascertainment. We tested whether cultural individualism predicts this variation independently of detection capacity, and whether the result is robust to known limitations of Hofstede's widely used but methodologically dated Individualism Index (IDV). Using 55 countries (GBD 2019 ASD prevalence, World Bank GDP, an author-constructed diagnostic infrastructure index, Hofstede's IDV, and a recently validated individualism-collectivism index built from nationally representative survey data; Akaliyski et al., 2025), we found the raw individualism-ASD correlation is robust to measurement choice (Hofstede: r = 0.702; validated index: r = 0.624; both p < .001, n = 47 non-screening countries with both measures available). However, its apparent independence from detection capacity is not robust: partial correlations controlling for GDP and diagnostic infrastructure remain significant with Hofstede's IDV (partial r = 0.30-0.39) but collapse to non-significance with the validated index (partial r = -0.14 to 0.09, ns), because the validated index correlates far more strongly with diagnostic infrastructure (r = 0.919) than Hofstede's IDV does (r = 0.818). The four mandatory-screening countries (Japan, South Korea, Singapore, Taiwan) exceed their IDV-predicted prevalence under both measures, though less dramatically using the validated index (1.57x vs. 2.84x), indicating measurement error in Hofstede's scores inflated the original screening-policy estimate. These findings show the bivariate cultural-prevalence association is genuine, but caution against treating it as evidence independent of detection capacity without testing robustness to cultural measurement choice.

title: Using Hierarchical Models to Estimate Heterogeneous Effects
abstract: Conditional theories are ubiquitous in political science, but standard interaction models cannot handle this proliferation of theoretically informed modifiers. This paper describes why, when, and how to use hierarchical models to encompass multiple sources of heterogeneity and regularize estimates. Doing so is simple, and starts with identifying the key sources of heterogeneity and grouping observations accordingly. Next, fit a hierarchical model with two linked regressions, one connecting treatment with the outcome, and another that models the treatment effects with potential sources of heterogeneity and partially pools group estimates. This captures systematic and random variation in heterogeneous effects, encompasses many interactions, and fits commonly used modeling frameworks, but regularization in this model breaks down if there are many small groups. I document these claims with a simulation analysis and reanalysis of a published study.

title: Theravada Buddhism in Contemporary China and Its Followers
abstract: This paper studies the influence of Theravada Buddhism in contemporary China, with a focus on the seven ethnic minorities that share a considerable presence of Theravada Buddhism. It also considers the populations of Theravada Buddhists among the seven ethnic minorities, as well as from another 49 official-recognized ethnicities. It discovers that the Theravada Buddhist population increases from 1.3868 million in 2010 to 1.4519 million in 2018 and is expected to grow to 1.4786 million by 2027. The present study finds that the Dai ethnicity is not only essential for spreading Theravada Buddhism to other ethnicities but it also has the largest Theravada Buddhist ethnicity in China, which represents more than 72% of the total Theravada Buddhist population. Finally, it discloses that the seven ethnicities each have their own forms of folk religions with their faith showing a mix of folk religion with Theravada Buddhism.

title: The Dai People and Their Relationship with Theravada Buddhists in Yunnan: A Profile and Population Analysis
abstract: Focusing on the Dai people of Yunnan, China, this study explores their demographics and Theravada Buddhist practices, examining their influence on neighboring ethnicities. It investigates how Theravada Buddhist temples serve as cornerstones of cultural identity and community cohesion, offering novel insights into the trajectory of Theravada Buddhism within Dai communities. The study employs two innovative approaches to estimate the Theravada Buddhist population in Yunnan and China. Firstly, it leverages data from the Pew Foundation survey conducted in neighboring countries. Secondly, it analyzes temple density in Xishuangbanna and Dehong. Both approaches converge on a figure of roughly 1.1 million Theravada Buddhists residing in Yunnan in 2016. Furthermore, the study estimates the total Theravada Buddhist population in Mainland China to be approximately 1.14 million in 2015 and 1.16 million in 2020.
