abstract: Tourism is increasingly promoted as a resource for health, and destinations market the well-being their landscapes are said to afford; yet the notion of well-being invoked where tourism and public health meet requires further specification, as the fields that converge there do not necessarily use the term in the same sense. The conceptual analysis clarifies well-being by distinguishing its psychological dimensions from its philosophical characterisation in terms of human flourishing, and frames health from a salutogenic perspective. Human flourishing and salutogenesis intersect particularly through meaningfulness and the ways persons engage with what places make possible. Drawing on the phenomenology of the tourist experience and on the literatures of therapeutic landscapes and restorative environments, the paper argues that places contribute to health through multiple and potentially interacting pathways involving characteristics of settings, activities and experiences, and their social and environmental contexts. Embodied pathways further show the interconnection of experiential and bodily dimensions of health. The paper draws out implications for public health and participatory destination design. Alpine tourism destinations provide a suitable context in which these relationships can be examined empirically.

title: Patient-reported experience as audit evidence: a new perspective on governance in integrated care
abstract: Patient-reported experience can identify problems in integrated care, yet feedback alone does not show whether organisations address them. This Perspective argues that experience data can inform internal audit evidence and person-centred healthcare governance when their quality, context and interpretive limits are examined. Developed within the author's doctoral research programme, the argument draws on a purposively selected set of scientific publications and official documents; it does not report a literature review or analyse the programme's empirical datasets. The conceptual method compares the purposes and units of patient-experience measurement, SCIROCCO integration maturity assessment, value-based healthcare implementation assessment and professional internal audit. An illustrative crosswalk then connects five coordination and participation concerns with contextual domains, candidate audit questions, corroborating information and management follow-up. The proposed cycle moves from patient-defined priorities through evidence evaluation to accountable action and repeated assessment of experience. It preserves management ownership of controls and distinguishes a reported concern from a demonstrated organisational failure. Neither the crosswalk nor the combined framework has been empirically validated. Patient involvement, feasibility assessment and comparative evaluation are needed to establish usefulness, burden and effects. The contribution is a testable governance proposition, not evidence of improved clinical outcomes or economic value. Keywords: patient-reported experience data, internal audit, audit evidence, integrated care, SCIROCCO maturity model, healthcare governance, person-centred care

title: Maternal Solidarity: Unconditional Cash Prescriptions and a Moral Economy of Motherhood in Flint, Michigan
authors: Caroline Doenmez, Jenny LaChance, Mallory Goldsworthy, Mona Hanna
abstract: How do mothers make meaning out of the experience of being “prescribed” no-strings-attached cash to improve their family’s health and life chances? This paper explores the impact of Rx Kids, the first community-wide cash transfer program for mothers and newborns in the United States. Launched in Flint, Michigan, in January 2024, the program seeks to “prescribe away” child poverty by providing cash transfers to mothers during and after their pregnancies. The program design stands apart from other cash transfer programs due to its universal and unconditional features: it ensures that all pregnant mothers in a participating community can receive the cash and does not impose any spending restrictions or reporting requirements on them. This paper is interested in Rx Kids’ cultural impact as ascertained through mothers’ narratives of their involvement with the program. Drawing on 46 interviews conducted with mothers in Flint, we ask: What did the unconditionality and universality of the program mean to them? Through their narratives, we identify how the transfer of monetary resources to the mothers elicited profound moral considerations. As mothers moved through the process of encountering, applying to, participating in, and advocating for the program, they narrated grappling continuously with the question of maternal worth and worthiness. Through their affective experiences of disbelief, astonishment, mistrust, anxiety, gratitude, and compassion for other mothers, we argue that the participants give voice to a moral economy of motherhood in Flint, circulating and contesting cultural values regarding reproductive labor and maternal worth. Ultimately, we show how through participating in the program, the mothers were actualized as both the recipients and providers of what we term “maternal solidarity,” an unconditional mode of care premised on a shared understanding of the pronounced and ubiquitous challenges of contemporary motherhood.

title: Blaming Across the Aisle: Political Contrasting and Blame Attribution in the Danish Parliament
authors: Markus Lundsfryd Jensen, Rune Egeskov Trust, Kenneth C. Enevoldsen, Sara Kolding
abstract: Political discourse is widely perceived to be growing more hostile, yet robust evidence remains scarce. This study examines blame attribution in the Danish Parliament from 1997 to 2026, combining a purpose-built classifier, BlameBERT (F1: 0.80), with multilevel statistical modeling. The classifier is constructed using an annotation-efficient pipeline for blame attribution in low-to-mid resource languages. The results reveal a banana-shaped trajectory, with blame declining until around 2016 before entering a significant and sustained increase in recent years (2019-2026). Government status consistently influenced blame attribution - an effect we term political contrasting - with opposition parties blaming substantially more than governing parties. This effect was moderated by ideology: The blame-dampening effect of governing was less pronounced among right-wing parties, and ideological extremity amplified blame more strongly on the right. In recent years, the interaction between political wing and ideological extremity intensified, suggesting an ideological hardening of the blame rhetoric concentrated on the right of the political spectrum. Taken together, these patterns suggest that the perceived rise in harsh political language reflects not merely a general rhetorical drift, but an ideologically asymmetric hardening of political discourse. A sensitivity analysis showed that the conclusions were robust to varying classification thresholds.

title: FRAGMENTED GOVERNANCE AND THE FAILURE TO EXECUTE URBAN PROJECTS: THE LARGO DA BATATA COMPETITION (2001-2022)
abstract: Architecture and urban design competitions are often defended as democratic selection mechanisms, yet many fail during implementation. This article argues the failure stems from fragmented governance: semi-autonomous sectoral authorities operating without a coordinating hierarchy. Through a 21-year documentary analysis of the National Competition for the Urban Reconversion of Largo da Batata (São Paulo), comparing the winning, basic and executed projects (2001-2022), we show each authority discharged its mandate competently, yet the absence of coordination fragmented the outcome. This mechanism, pockets of micro-regulation practices, moves the debate from describing competition failure to explaining it, with implications for governance research.

title: Heed the warning: how NATO can find and fill the gaps in its warning systems
abstract: Intelligence warning failures are too often viewed in binary: Either intelligence succeeded or it failed. In reality, often only segments of the warning chain collapse while others operate well. This Outlook paper treats warning success as a spectrum rather than as a pass/fail test in a new framework for warning performance. It illustrates the use through three recent case studies: the fall of Kabul (2021), Russia’s invasion of Ukraine (2022) and the Niger coup (2023). The decisive shortfall across all three cases was the failure to reconcile divergent NATO member state views into an operational consensus within NATO. There are practical solutions for integrating NATO capabilities to institutionalize rapid after-action reviews, conduct periodic divergence drill exercises, prepare contingency packages and further embed red team analyses.
